cards.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle comes immediately after isovolumetric contraction?
cards.a: Ventricular ejection.
options: Isovolumetric relaxation
Atrial systole
Ventricular ejection
Rapid ventricular filling
cards.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction ends the moment ventricular pressure climbs above aortic pressure, the semilunar valve opens, and ejection begins. Atrial systole comes before isovolumetric contraction, not after. Isovolumetric relaxation follows ejection, once the semilunar valve has closed. Rapid ventricular filling follows isovolumetric relaxation, after the AV valve opens.

cards.q: Which valves are open during isovolumetric contraction?
cards.a: None of them.
options: None of them
The semilunar valves only
The AV valves only
All four valves
cards.explanation: Isovolumetric means the volume cannot change, and volume can only stay fixed if no valve is open. The AV valves have just closed because ventricular pressure passed atrial pressure, and the semilunar valves have not yet opened because ventricular pressure is still below arterial pressure. The AV valves open only during filling and the semilunar valves only during ejection, so neither pair is open here.

cards.q: What pressure relationship opens the aortic valve?
cards.a: Left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure.
options: Left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure
Aortic pressure rises above left ventricular pressure
Left atrial pressure rises above left ventricular pressure
Left ventricular pressure falls below left atrial pressure
cards.explanation: Valves are passive, so each one opens whenever the pressure behind it exceeds the pressure in front of it. For the aortic valve, behind means the ventricle and in front means the aorta, so the ventricle must win. Aortic pressure exceeding ventricular pressure is what closes that valve instead. The two options involving the atrium describe the mitral valve, which opens when the atrium wins and closes when the ventricle does.

cards.q: What pressure relationship closes the atrioventricular valves?
cards.a: Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure.
options: Atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure
Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure
Aortic pressure falls below ventricular pressure
Ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure
cards.explanation: As the ventricle begins to contract its pressure crosses above atrial pressure, and the backward push snaps the AV cusps shut. Atrial pressure exceeding ventricular pressure is the opposite condition and is what opens those valves during filling. The two aortic comparisons govern the semilunar valve, not the AV valve: the ventricle winning opens it and the aorta winning closes it.

cards.q: Atrial systole contributes the final portion of which volume?
cards.a: End diastolic volume.
options: Stroke volume
End systolic volume
Cardiac reserve
End diastolic volume
cards.explanation: Atrial contraction tops off the ventricle at the very end of filling, adding roughly the last twenty percent of what the ventricle holds when the AV valve closes, which is the end diastolic volume by definition. Stroke volume is what leaves during ejection, not what is present at the end of filling. End systolic volume is the leftover after ejection. Cardiac reserve is the difference between maximum and resting cardiac output and has nothing to do with a single filling phase.

cards.q: Ventricular volume sits at end systolic volume throughout which phase?
cards.a: Isovolumetric relaxation.
options: Reduced ejection
Isovolumetric relaxation
Rapid ventricular filling
Isovolumetric contraction
cards.explanation: Ejection ends when the semilunar valve closes, leaving end systolic volume behind, and that volume cannot change until the AV valve opens, so it holds constant through isovolumetric relaxation. During reduced ejection the volume is still falling toward end systolic volume. During rapid filling it is climbing away from it. Isovolumetric contraction also holds volume constant, but at end diastolic volume, the largest volume of the cycle rather than the smallest.

cards.q: What pressure relationship closes the semilunar valves?
cards.a: Arterial pressure rises above ventricular pressure.
options: Ventricular pressure rises above arterial pressure
Arterial pressure rises above ventricular pressure
Atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure
Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure
cards.explanation: Late in ejection the relaxing ventricle loses pressure faster than the elastic artery does, the gradient reverses, and backflow catches the semilunar cusps and shuts them. The ventricle winning over the artery is the condition that opened the valve a moment earlier. The two options comparing the atrium and ventricle describe AV valve events during filling, which happen after the semilunar valve is already closed.

cards.q: At a resting heart rate of about 70 beats per minute, which portion of the cardiac cycle is longest?
cards.a: Ventricular filling.
options: Isovolumetric contraction
Ventricular ejection
Ventricular filling
Isovolumetric relaxation
cards.explanation: At rest a cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds, and roughly two thirds of that is diastole, most of which is ventricular filling. Isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation each take only a few hundredths of a second because they last only as long as it takes pressure to cross a threshold. Ejection takes about 0.25 seconds, long but still shorter than filling. This is why speeding the heart cuts into filling first.

cards.q: Left ventricular pressure is 15 mmHg and rising, left atrial pressure is 8 mmHg, and aortic pressure is 80 mmHg. Which phase is this?
cards.a: Isovolumetric contraction.
options: Rapid ventricular filling
Isovolumetric contraction
Atrial systole
Ventricular ejection
cards.explanation: Compare each valve separately. The ventricle at 15 mmHg beats the atrium at 8 mmHg, so the mitral valve is shut, and the ventricle is far below the aorta at 80 mmHg, so the aortic valve is also shut. Both valves closed with pressure climbing is isovolumetric contraction. Filling and atrial systole both require the atrium to exceed the ventricle, and ejection requires the ventricle to exceed the aorta.

cards.q: Left ventricular pressure is 112 mmHg and aortic pressure is 104 mmHg. What is happening at the aortic valve?
cards.a: It is open and blood is being ejected.
options: It is closed because the aorta holds the higher pressure
It is open and blood is being ejected
It is closed because the ventricle is relaxing
It is fluttering shut as the ventricle fills
cards.explanation: The ventricle exceeds the aorta by 8 mmHg, so the gradient points outward and the valve stands open with flow moving into the aorta. The aorta does not hold the higher pressure here, so that reading contradicts the numbers given. Ventricular relaxation would only close the valve once aortic pressure had climbed back above ventricular pressure, which has not happened yet. The aortic valve plays no part in ventricular filling.

cards.q: Left atrial pressure is 10 mmHg and left ventricular pressure is 4 mmHg. What is the state of the mitral valve and the ventricular volume?
cards.a: Open, with volume increasing.
options: Closed, with volume constant
Open, with volume decreasing
Closed, with volume decreasing
Open, with volume increasing
cards.explanation: The atrium exceeds the ventricle by 6 mmHg, so the mitral valve is held open and blood runs down the gradient into the ventricle, which means volume is rising. Closed with constant volume would describe either isovolumetric phase, but those require the ventricle to hold the higher pressure. Volume can only decrease during ejection, which needs an open semilunar valve, and an open mitral valve with falling volume would mean blood was running backward into the atrium.

cards.q: Heart rate climbs from 70 to 160 beats per minute. Which part of the cardiac cycle is shortened the most?
cards.a: Ventricular filling.
options: Isovolumetric contraction
Ventricular ejection
Ventricular filling
Isovolumetric relaxation
cards.explanation: Systole is relatively protected as rate climbs because contraction and relaxation are driven by fixed calcium handling steps, so most of the lost time comes out of diastole, and filling is by far the largest piece of diastole. Isovolumetric contraction and relaxation are already only a few hundredths of a second each and have little to give up. Ejection shortens somewhat but far less than filling, which is why very fast rates lower end diastolic volume.

cards.q: The dicrotic notch on an aortic pressure tracing marks which event?
cards.a: Closure of the aortic valve.
options: Closure of the mitral valve
Opening of the aortic valve
Closure of the aortic valve
Opening of the mitral valve
cards.explanation: As the ventricle relaxes, a brief backflow toward the ventricle dips aortic pressure, then the aortic cusps catch that flow and slam shut, producing the small rebound notch. Mitral closure happens at the start of systole and is not visible on an aortic tracing. Aortic valve opening produces the sharp upstroke at the beginning of ejection, not a notch on the downslope. Mitral opening occurs later, once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.

cards.q: Blood flow through the coronary arteries feeding the left ventricular wall is greatest during which part of the cycle?
cards.a: Diastole, while the ventricle is relaxed.
options: Systole, while the ventricle is contracting
Diastole, while the ventricle is relaxed
Isovolumetric contraction specifically
Peak ejection specifically
cards.explanation: The coronary vessels run through the ventricular wall, so contraction squeezes them shut and flow is highest when the muscle is relaxed and aortic pressure is still elevated, which is diastole. Systole, including isovolumetric contraction and peak ejection, is exactly when wall compression is greatest and left coronary flow is at its lowest. This is why very fast heart rates, which cut diastolic time, threaten coronary perfusion.

cards.q: If the mitral valve failed to close at the start of ventricular contraction, what would happen during isovolumetric contraction?
cards.a: Blood would be driven backward into the left atrium, so volume would fall.
options: Volume would stay constant but pressure would rise faster than normal
Ventricular filling would continue through the phase from the atrium
The aortic valve would open earlier than normal because pressure rises faster
Blood would be driven backward into the left atrium, so volume would fall
cards.explanation: The phase is isovolumetric only because both valves seal, so with the mitral valve leaking the contracting ventricle has a low pressure escape route into the atrium, volume falls, and the phase stops being isovolumetric. Pressure would rise more slowly, not faster, because the ventricle is unloading. The aortic valve would open later, not earlier, since it takes longer to build the pressure needed. Filling requires atrial pressure to exceed ventricular pressure, which is not the case once contraction begins.

cards.q: A runner's heart rate rises to 180 beats per minute and venous return does not increase enough to compensate. Trace the effect on filling time, end diastolic volume, and stroke volume.
cards.a: Filling time falls, end diastolic volume falls, and stroke volume falls.
options: Filling time falls, end diastolic volume falls, and stroke volume falls
Filling time falls, end diastolic volume rises, and stroke volume rises
Filling time rises, end diastolic volume falls, and stroke volume rises
Filling time falls, end diastolic volume is unchanged, and stroke volume falls
cards.explanation: A faster rate shortens the cycle and diastole absorbs most of the loss, so the ventricle has less time to fill and end diastolic volume drops. By the Frank Starling relationship a smaller end diastolic volume means less stretch and a weaker ejection, so stroke volume falls too. End diastolic volume cannot rise on less filling time without a larger venous return, which the question excludes, and it cannot stay unchanged for the same reason. Filling time must fall, not rise, when the cycle shortens.

cards.q: A drug constricts the systemic arterioles and raises aortic diastolic pressure from 80 to 110 mmHg. What happens to the duration of isovolumetric contraction and to the timing of aortic valve opening?
cards.a: Isovolumetric contraction lengthens and the aortic valve opens later.
options: Isovolumetric contraction lengthens and the aortic valve opens later
Isovolumetric contraction shortens and the aortic valve opens earlier
Isovolumetric contraction lengthens and the aortic valve opens earlier
Isovolumetric contraction is unchanged and the aortic valve opens later
cards.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction lasts exactly as long as it takes ventricular pressure to climb from atrial pressure up to aortic pressure. Raising the aortic threshold by 30 mmHg means more time is spent building pressure, so the phase lengthens and the valve opens later in the beat. A shorter phase with earlier opening is what a lower aortic pressure would produce. The phase cannot lengthen and open earlier at once, since those are the same event described two ways, and it cannot be unchanged when the threshold it must reach has moved.

cards.q: On a recording, ventricular pressure climbs steeply while ventricular volume holds flat, and then volume falls sharply while pressure keeps climbing. Which two phases are shown, and what valve event separates them?
cards.a: Isovolumetric contraction then ejection, separated by semilunar valve opening.
options: Isovolumetric relaxation then filling, separated by AV valve opening
Isovolumetric contraction then ejection, separated by semilunar valve opening
Ejection then isovolumetric relaxation, separated by semilunar valve closure
Filling then isovolumetric contraction, separated by AV valve closure
cards.explanation: Flat volume with rising pressure can only be isovolumetric contraction, since relaxation drops pressure instead, and falling volume means blood is leaving, which is ejection. The only event that lets volume start falling is the semilunar valve opening once the ventricle outpressures the artery. Isovolumetric relaxation into filling would show pressure falling rather than rising, and filling into isovolumetric contraction would show volume rising first. Ejection into relaxation would show volume fall first and then flatten.

cards.q: A patient develops atrial fibrillation, so organized atrial systole is lost while ventricular contraction continues. Predict the effect on end diastolic volume and stroke volume, and when the loss matters most.
cards.a: Both fall modestly, and the loss matters most at high heart rates.
options: Both fall modestly, and the loss matters most at high heart rates
Both fall modestly, and the loss matters most at low heart rates
Both rise, because the ventricle fills for longer
End diastolic volume falls but stroke volume is unchanged
cards.explanation: Atrial systole adds only the last fifth or so of end diastolic volume, so losing it trims filling modestly, and a smaller end diastolic volume gives a smaller stroke volume through the Frank Starling relationship. The loss bites hardest when the heart is fast, because passive filling time is already short and the atrial contribution is proportionally larger. At slow rates there is ample time for passive filling to make up the difference. Volumes cannot rise when a filling contribution is removed, and stroke volume cannot hold steady when preload has dropped.

cards.q: On a ventricular pressure volume loop, what does the width of the loop measure?
cards.a: Stroke volume.
options: Stroke volume
End diastolic volume
End systolic volume
Stroke work
cards.explanation: The loop runs from end diastolic volume on the right to end systolic volume on the left, so the horizontal distance between those corners is exactly the volume ejected, which is stroke volume. End diastolic volume is the position of the right edge, not the width, and end systolic volume is the position of the left edge. Stroke work is the area enclosed by the loop, which depends on both width and height.

cards.q: Which segment of the pressure volume loop is vertical with pressure rising and volume unchanged?
cards.a: Isovolumetric contraction.
options: Ventricular filling
Ejection
Isovolumetric contraction
Isovolumetric relaxation
cards.explanation: A vertical segment means volume is fixed, which happens only when all valves are shut, and rising pressure identifies the contracting side of the loop. Isovolumetric relaxation is also vertical but pressure is falling there, so it is the descending limb on the left. Filling is the roughly horizontal bottom of the loop where volume rises at low pressure. Ejection is the top of the loop where volume falls.

cards.q: The lower right corner of the pressure volume loop marks which event?
cards.a: Mitral valve closure at end diastolic volume.
options: Aortic valve closure at end systolic volume
Aortic valve opening at end diastolic volume
Mitral valve closure at end diastolic volume
Mitral valve opening at end systolic volume
cards.explanation: Filling runs rightward along the bottom of the loop and stops at the largest volume of the cycle, where the ventricle starts to contract and the mitral valve shuts, so that corner is end diastolic volume. Aortic valve closure sits at the upper left corner at end systolic volume. Aortic valve opening is at the top of the vertical contraction limb, at end diastolic volume but at high pressure. Mitral valve opening is the lower left corner where filling begins.

cards.q: The upper left corner of the loop, where ejection ends, corresponds to which volume?
cards.a: End systolic volume.
options: End systolic volume
End diastolic volume
Stroke volume
Residual filling volume
cards.explanation: Ejection moves the loop leftward as volume falls, and it stops when the aortic valve closes, leaving behind whatever the ventricle could not eject, which is end systolic volume. End diastolic volume is the opposite corner at the far right of the loop. Stroke volume is a difference between the two corners rather than a point on the loop. Residual filling volume is not a standard term in this framework.

cards.q: The end systolic pressure volume relationship, the line touching the upper left corners of loops recorded at different loads, indexes which property?
cards.a: Contractility.
options: Contractility
Afterload
Preload
Ventricular compliance
cards.explanation: Because that line is defined by where ejection stops regardless of how the ventricle was loaded, its slope reports the intrinsic strength of the muscle, which is contractility. Preload is read on the volume axis at the right lower corner, not from this line. Afterload is read as the pressure at which the aortic valve opens. Compliance is described by the end diastolic pressure volume relationship along the bottom of the loop instead.

cards.q: The end diastolic pressure volume relationship, the curve along the bottom of the loop, describes what property of the ventricle?
cards.a: Its passive compliance during filling.
options: The rate of calcium release per beat
Its maximum contractile force
The arterial load it ejects against
Its passive compliance during filling
cards.explanation: The bottom of the loop is traced while the muscle is relaxed, so the pressure recorded at each volume reflects how easily the resting wall stretches, which is compliance. Maximum contractile force is reported by the end systolic relationship at the top left instead. Arterial load is seen as the pressure at which the loop turns and ejection begins. Calcium release per beat influences contractility, which shows up on the systolic side of the loop, not the passive filling curve.

cards.q: The area enclosed inside the pressure volume loop represents what?
cards.a: Stroke work done by the ventricle in that beat.
options: Ejection fraction for that beat
The compliance of the ventricular wall
Cardiac output over one minute
Stroke work done by the ventricle in that beat
cards.explanation: Work is pressure multiplied by a volume change, so the enclosed area, which combines the pressure developed with the volume moved, is the external work of one beat. Ejection fraction is a ratio of two volumes and carries no pressure information. Cardiac output is a per minute flow and needs heart rate, which no single loop contains. Compliance is a slope on the filling curve, not an enclosed area.

cards.q: Which valve opens at the transition from the vertical rising limb of the loop to the ejection segment?
cards.a: The aortic valve.
options: The aortic valve
The tricuspid valve
The mitral valve
The pulmonic valve
cards.explanation: On a left ventricular loop, ejection starts when ventricular pressure passes aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens, ending the isovolumetric climb. The mitral valve opens at the bottom left corner to begin filling. The tricuspid and pulmonic valves belong to the right ventricle, which has its own loop at much lower pressures.

cards.q: Venous return increases while arterial pressure and contractility are held constant. How does the loop change?
cards.a: It widens to the right, with a larger end diastolic volume and larger stroke volume.
options: It narrows, with a higher end systolic volume and smaller stroke volume
It shifts leftward, with a lower end systolic volume and larger stroke volume
It widens to the right, with a larger end diastolic volume and larger stroke volume
It grows taller, with a higher pressure at aortic valve opening
cards.explanation: More venous return is a pure preload increase, so the filling limb runs further right and the loop starts contracting from a larger end diastolic volume, and Frank Starling turns that extra stretch into a larger stroke volume with end systolic volume nearly unchanged. Narrowing with a higher end systolic volume is the afterload response. A leftward shift with a lower end systolic volume is the contractility response. A higher pressure at aortic valve opening also signals afterload, not preload.

cards.q: Aortic pressure is raised while venous return and contractility are held constant. How does the loop change?
cards.a: The aortic valve opens at a higher pressure, end systolic volume rises, and the loop narrows.
options: End systolic volume falls and the upper left corner moves left along a steeper line
The aortic valve opens at a higher pressure, end systolic volume falls, and the loop widens
End diastolic volume rises immediately and the loop widens to the right
The aortic valve opens at a higher pressure, end systolic volume rises, and the loop narrows
cards.explanation: A higher arterial pressure means the ventricle must climb higher before the valve opens, and because it is ejecting against more resistance it stops sooner, leaving more blood behind, so end systolic volume rises and the width, which is stroke volume, shrinks. End systolic volume cannot fall when ejection is opposed more strongly. An immediate rightward shift of end diastolic volume is the preload change, not the afterload change, though preload does rise on later beats. A leftward move along a steeper end systolic line is the signature of increased contractility.

cards.q: Contractility increases while preload and afterload are held constant. How does the loop change?
cards.a: End systolic volume falls, the loop widens, and the end systolic line steepens.
options: End diastolic volume falls, the loop narrows, and stroke volume falls
End systolic volume rises, the loop narrows, and stroke volume falls
End systolic volume falls, the loop widens, and the end systolic line steepens
End diastolic volume rises and the end diastolic filling curve shifts upward
cards.explanation: Greater contractility lets the ventricle keep ejecting to a smaller residual volume at the same load, so the upper left corner moves left, the loop widens, and the line describing where ejection stops tilts steeper. A falling end diastolic volume with a narrower loop describes reduced preload. A rising end systolic volume with a narrow loop is the afterload or the failing heart pattern. A shifted end diastolic curve describes a change in passive stiffness, which is a diastolic property rather than contractility.

cards.q: Only preload is increased. Which corner of the loop moves first?
cards.a: The lower right corner, at end diastolic volume.
options: The upper left corner, at end systolic volume
The lower left corner, where the mitral valve opens
The lower right corner, at end diastolic volume
The top of the ejection segment, at peak pressure
cards.explanation: Preload is defined by how full the ventricle is when contraction begins, so the first thing to move is the point where filling ends and the mitral valve closes, the lower right corner. The upper left corner is set mainly by contractility and afterload and shifts little with pure preload change. The lower left corner is where the previous beat ended. Peak ejection pressure follows from the arterial load rather than from filling volume alone.

cards.q: Two loops from the same ventricle share the same end diastolic volume, but one turns and opens the aortic valve at 80 mmHg and the other at 120 mmHg. Which variable differs?
cards.a: Afterload.
options: Preload
Afterload
Contractility
Ventricular compliance
cards.explanation: The pressure at which the loop turns from the vertical limb into ejection is the arterial pressure the ventricle must overcome, which is afterload, so a 40 mmHg difference in that threshold is an afterload difference. Preload is identical here, because both loops share an end diastolic volume. Contractility would show as a difference in where ejection stops rather than where it starts. Compliance would show as a different height of the filling curve along the bottom.

cards.q: A ventricle becomes stiffer during diastole while contractility is unchanged. How does the loop change?
cards.a: The filling curve rises, so a given volume sits at a higher pressure.
options: The end systolic pressure volume line becomes steeper than before
The filling curve rises, so a given volume sits at a higher pressure
The aortic valve opens at a lower pressure than it did before
The loop becomes wider at the same end diastolic volume
cards.explanation: Stiffness is low compliance, so the passive wall generates more pressure for each milliliter admitted and the bottom curve of the loop sits higher, which is also why filling volumes tend to fall. A steeper end systolic line would mean contractility had risen, which the question excludes. Aortic valve opening pressure is set by arterial load, not by diastolic stiffness. A wider loop at the same end diastolic volume would require more contractility or less afterload.

cards.q: Compared with a control loop, a second loop from the same ventricle starts contracting at the same end diastolic volume but ends ejection at a smaller end systolic volume and reaches a higher peak pressure. Which change explains it, and what happens to ejection fraction?
cards.a: Increased contractility, and ejection fraction rises.
options: Increased contractility, and ejection fraction rises
Increased afterload, and ejection fraction falls
Increased preload, and ejection fraction is unchanged
Decreased contractility, and ejection fraction falls
cards.explanation: An unchanged end diastolic volume rules out a preload change, and a smaller end systolic volume with more pressure generated is the definition of a stronger beat, so contractility has risen. Since ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end diastolic volume, and the numerator grew while the denominator held, the fraction rises. Increased afterload would leave more blood behind, not less. Decreased contractility would raise end systolic volume and lower peak pressure.

cards.q: A loop is recorded with end diastolic volume 120 mL and end systolic volume 50 mL. Afterload is then raised and end systolic volume becomes 70 mL with end diastolic volume still 120 mL. Calculate stroke volume and ejection fraction before and after.
cards.a: 70 mL and 58 percent before, 50 mL and 42 percent after.
options: 70 mL and 42 percent before, 50 mL and 58 percent after
70 mL and 58 percent before, 50 mL and 42 percent after
50 mL and 58 percent before, 70 mL and 42 percent after
70 mL and 58 percent before, 70 mL and 42 percent after
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is end diastolic minus end systolic volume, so 120 minus 50 is 70 mL, and 120 minus 70 is 50 mL. Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end diastolic volume, giving 70 divided by 120, about 58 percent, and 50 divided by 120, about 42 percent. One distractor swaps the two fractions, another swaps the stroke volumes, and another holds stroke volume fixed even though end systolic volume changed, which is arithmetically impossible.

cards.q: Afterload is raised suddenly and venous return continues unchanged. Trace what the loop does on the very next beat and then over the following several beats.
cards.a: End systolic volume rises at once, then end diastolic volume rises and stroke volume partly recovers.
options: End systolic volume falls at once, then end diastolic volume falls and stroke volume recovers fully
End systolic volume rises at once, then end diastolic volume rises and stroke volume partly recovers
End diastolic volume rises first, then end systolic volume falls and stroke volume rises above baseline
End systolic volume rises at once and then keeps rising with no change in end diastolic volume
cards.explanation: The immediate effect of more afterload is incomplete emptying, so end systolic volume climbs and the loop narrows. On the next beats that leftover blood adds to the unchanged venous return, so end diastolic volume rises, the extra stretch recruits Frank Starling, and stroke volume climbs back toward but not all the way to baseline. End systolic volume cannot fall when ejection is opposed more strongly. Preload rises as a consequence here, not first, and end diastolic volume cannot stay fixed while residual volume accumulates.

cards.q: Two loops are recorded from one ventricle. They share the same end systolic pressure volume line and the same aortic valve opening pressure, but the second loop is wider and its right edge sits further right. What changed?
cards.a: Preload rose, moving the loop along an unchanged contractile state.
options: Preload rose, moving the loop along an unchanged contractile state
Contractility rose, because the loop became wider than before
Afterload fell, because more volume was ejected each beat
Compliance fell, because end diastolic volume increased further
cards.explanation: A shared end systolic line means the contractile state is identical, and a shared opening pressure means the arterial load is identical, so the only thing left that can move the right edge outward is more filling, which is preload. A wider loop alone does not prove more contractility, since Frank Starling widens the loop at constant contractility, and that is exactly the confusion this pair of loops is built to expose. Falling afterload would lower the pressure at which ejection began. Falling compliance would make the ventricle harder to fill, shifting the right edge left rather than right.

cards.q: What produces the first heart sound?
cards.a: Closure of the atrioventricular valves.
options: Closure of the atrioventricular valves
Closure of the semilunar valves
Opening of the semilunar valves
Contraction of the atrial muscle
cards.explanation: As the ventricles begin to contract, ventricular pressure passes atrial pressure, the mitral and tricuspid valves shut, and the vibration of the sealed valve and the blood behind it makes the first sound. Semilunar closure makes the second sound at the end of ejection. Valve opening is normally silent because it does not create the abrupt tensioning that generates sound. Atrial contraction is also normally silent in a compliant ventricle.

cards.q: What produces the second heart sound?
cards.a: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves.
options: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
Turbulence as blood enters the ventricle
cards.explanation: When the ventricles relax, arterial pressure overtakes ventricular pressure and the semilunar valves snap shut, producing the second sound and marking the end of ejection. Mitral and tricuspid closure produce the first sound at the start of systole. Normal valve opening does not generate an audible sound. Turbulence during filling can produce a third sound in some hearts, but that is a separate finding from the second sound.

cards.q: The first heart sound marks the beginning of which phase?
cards.a: Isovolumetric contraction.
options: Ventricular filling
Isovolumetric contraction
Reduced ejection
Isovolumetric relaxation
cards.explanation: The AV valves close at the instant ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, and with the semilunar valves still shut the ventricle enters isovolumetric contraction, so the sound and the phase start together. Ventricular filling begins later, when the AV valve opens after the second sound. Isovolumetric relaxation begins at the second sound, not the first. Ejection begins after isovolumetric contraction, when the semilunar valve opens, and is silent in a normal heart.

cards.q: The second heart sound marks the beginning of which phase?
cards.a: Isovolumetric relaxation.
options: Rapid ventricular filling
Isovolumetric relaxation
Atrial systole
Ventricular ejection
cards.explanation: The second sound is semilunar valve closure, which ends ejection and leaves both valve pairs shut while the ventricle relaxes, which is isovolumetric relaxation. Rapid filling starts a little later, once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure and the AV valve opens. Atrial systole occurs at the very end of filling, just before the first sound. Ejection ends at the second sound rather than beginning with it.

cards.q: A murmur heard between the first and second heart sounds is described as what?
cards.a: Systolic.
options: Systolic
Diastolic
Continuous
Presystolic
cards.explanation: The interval bounded by AV valve closure and semilunar valve closure is ventricular systole by definition, so a sound in that window is systolic. A diastolic murmur falls in the opposite interval, after the second sound and before the next first sound. A continuous murmur spans both intervals without stopping at the second sound. Presystolic refers to the very end of diastole during atrial contraction, which is still before the first sound.

cards.q: Aortic stenosis produces a murmur with what timing?
cards.a: Systolic, while blood is forced through the narrowed valve.
options: Diastolic, while blood leaks backward through the closed valve
Only during atrial contraction at the end of filling
Continuous, spanning both systole and diastole without pause
Systolic, while blood is forced through the narrowed valve
cards.explanation: A stenotic valve is noisy when it is supposed to be open and carrying flow, and the aortic valve carries flow during ejection, so the murmur falls in systole. A diastolic leak through the aortic valve describes regurgitation, not stenosis, and is the useful contrast to keep straight. A continuous murmur suggests an abnormal connection carrying flow all cycle. Atrial contraction does not drive blood through the aortic valve at all.

cards.q: Mitral regurgitation produces a murmur with what timing?
cards.a: Systolic, while the ventricle drives blood back through it.
options: Systolic, while the ventricle drives blood back through it
Diastolic, while the ventricle fills through the valve
Only at the moment the second heart sound is produced
Only during isovolumetric relaxation after ejection
cards.explanation: A regurgitant valve is noisy when it is supposed to be shut, and the mitral valve is shut during ventricular systole, so the leak is heard between the first and second sounds. A diastolic murmur across the mitral valve would instead point to mitral stenosis, since that is when the valve should be open and carrying flow. The second sound is a single brief event, not the span of a murmur, and isovolumetric relaxation follows systole rather than containing it.

cards.q: A third heart sound occurs during which event?
cards.a: Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole.
options: Atrial contraction at the end of diastole
The peak of ventricular ejection
Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole
Isovolumetric contraction
cards.explanation: The third sound is a low pitched thud made as a rush of blood decelerates against the ventricular wall just after the AV valve opens, which is early diastolic rapid filling. Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces the fourth sound instead, which is the pairing students most often reverse. Ejection and isovolumetric contraction are systolic events and are silent in a normal heart.

cards.q: A murmur is heard clearly between the first and second heart sounds. Which pair of lesions could produce it?
cards.a: Aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation.
options: Aortic regurgitation or mitral stenosis
Aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation
Aortic stenosis or mitral stenosis
Aortic regurgitation or mitral regurgitation
cards.explanation: During systole the semilunar valves are open and carrying flow, so narrowing there is noisy, while the AV valves are shut, so leaking there is noisy. That gives aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation. Aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis are both diastolic for the mirror image reason. The mixed options each pair one systolic lesion with one diastolic lesion, so they cannot both fall in the same window.

cards.q: A murmur begins right after the second heart sound and fades before the next first sound. Which lesion fits?
cards.a: Aortic regurgitation.
options: Aortic stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation
Pulmonic stenosis
cards.explanation: The window after the second sound is diastole, when the aortic valve should be sealed, so blood running back from the aorta into the relaxing ventricle produces exactly this decreasing murmur. Aortic stenosis and pulmonic stenosis both make noise while their valves carry ejected blood, so both are systolic. Mitral regurgitation is also systolic, because the mitral valve is shut only while the ventricle contracts.

cards.q: Which general rule links a valve lesion to the timing of its murmur?
cards.a: A stenotic valve is noisy when it should be open, and a regurgitant valve is noisy when it should be closed.
options: A stenotic valve is noisy when it should be closed, and a regurgitant valve is noisy when it should be open
Both stenosis and regurgitation are noisy when the valve should be closed
Both stenosis and regurgitation are noisy when the valve should be open
A stenotic valve is noisy when it should be open, and a regurgitant valve is noisy when it should be closed
cards.explanation: Turbulence needs flow through a place it does not fit, so narrowing is heard while the valve is carrying its normal forward flow, and incompetence is heard while pressure is trying to push blood back through a seal that fails. Reversing the two predicts the wrong half of the cycle for every lesion. Assigning both lesions to the same phase ignores that stenosis and regurgitation are opposite failures of the same valve.

cards.q: Why does the second heart sound normally split during inspiration?
cards.a: Increased venous return prolongs right ventricular ejection, so the pulmonic valve closes later.
options: Increased venous return prolongs right ventricular ejection, so the pulmonic valve closes later
Falling venous return shortens right ventricular ejection, so the pulmonic valve closes earlier
The aortic valve closes later because systemic pressure rises during inspiration
The mitral and tricuspid valves close at different times during inspiration
cards.explanation: Inspiration drops intrathoracic pressure, which pulls more blood into the right heart, and the larger right ventricular volume takes longer to eject, delaying pulmonic closure and separating the two components of the second sound. Venous return rises rather than falls with inspiration, so any answer built on falling venous return has the direction backward. Systemic pressure does not rise enough to delay aortic closure, and in fact left sided filling is slightly reduced. Splitting of the first sound involves the AV valves and is a separate phenomenon.

cards.q: A fourth heart sound is heard just before the first heart sound. What does it indicate about the ventricle?
cards.a: The ventricle is stiff, so atrial contraction meets a resistant chamber.
options: The ventricle is unusually compliant, so it accepts blood too easily
The ventricle is stiff, so atrial contraction meets a resistant chamber
The semilunar valve is closing later than the other semilunar valve
The ventricle is ejecting against an unusually low arterial load
cards.explanation: The fourth sound comes from atrial systole meeting resistance, so it reports a ventricle whose passive filling curve is shifted up, meaning low compliance. An unusually compliant ventricle absorbs the atrial kick silently. Late semilunar closure alters the second sound, which sits at the other end of systole. Afterload governs ejection and does not create a sound just before the first sound.

cards.q: At a resting heart rate, the interval between the second sound and the next first sound is longer than the interval between the first and second sounds. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The longer pause is diastole, so a murmur falling in it is diastolic.
options: The longer pause is systole, so a murmur falling in it is systolic
The two intervals are equal, so timing cannot be judged by ear
The longer pause is diastole, so a murmur falling in it is diastolic
The longer pause is isovolumetric relaxation
cards.explanation: Systole runs from the first sound to the second sound, and at rest it occupies roughly a third of the cycle, so the remaining gap back to the next first sound is the longer one and is diastole. Calling the long pause systole reverses the two and misdates every murmur. The intervals are plainly unequal at rest, which is exactly what makes timing by ear possible. Isovolumetric relaxation is only the first few hundredths of a second of that long pause, not the whole of it.

cards.q: As heart rate rises toward 170 beats per minute, why does telling the first sound from the second by rhythm alone become unreliable?
cards.a: Diastole shortens toward the length of systole, so the two pauses become nearly equal.
options: Diastole shortens toward the length of systole, so the two pauses become nearly equal
Systole shortens toward the length of diastole, so the two pauses become nearly equal
Both sounds disappear at high rates
The first sound moves into diastole at high rates
cards.explanation: Speeding the heart takes its time mainly out of diastole, so the long pause shrinks until it resembles the short one and the rhythmic cue that identifies the first sound is gone. Systole is comparatively protected, so it is not the interval that collapses. The sounds get harder to separate but do not vanish. The first sound is defined by AV valve closure at the start of systole and cannot migrate into diastole.

cards.q: A harsh murmur fills the interval between the first and second sounds, and a catheter shows left ventricular pressure of 190 mmHg during ejection while aortic pressure is only 115 mmHg. What lesion is this, and what has happened to the left ventricle's afterload?
cards.a: Aortic stenosis, and afterload is increased by the pressure gradient across the valve.
options: Mitral regurgitation, and afterload is decreased because blood escapes into the atrium
Aortic stenosis, and afterload is increased by the pressure gradient across the valve
Aortic regurgitation, and afterload is unchanged because the leak occurs in diastole
Mitral stenosis, and afterload is increased because filling pressure is high
cards.explanation: A systolic murmur plus a 75 mmHg pressure drop across the aortic valve during ejection means the valve orifice is narrowed, and the ventricle now faces the arterial pressure plus that gradient, so its load during ejection is much larger than the cuff pressure suggests. Mitral regurgitation does lower afterload by offering a low pressure escape route, so its direction is opposite. Aortic regurgitation is diastolic and would not create a systolic gradient. Mitral stenosis raises the pressure the atrium must generate, which is a filling problem rather than an ejection load.

cards.q: A patient has a decreasing murmur that starts immediately after the second sound. Over months, what happens to left ventricular end diastolic volume and to arterial pulse pressure?
cards.a: End diastolic volume rises and pulse pressure widens.
options: End diastolic volume falls and pulse pressure narrows
End diastolic volume rises and pulse pressure widens
End diastolic volume rises and pulse pressure narrows
End diastolic volume is unchanged and pulse pressure widens
cards.explanation: A murmur beginning right after the second sound is aortic regurgitation, so during diastole the ventricle receives blood from the atrium and from the aorta at once, which enlarges end diastolic volume. Meanwhile the aorta is drained backward during diastole so diastolic pressure falls, while the larger total stroke volume raises systolic pressure, and pulse pressure widens on both counts. End diastolic volume cannot fall when the ventricle is being filled from two directions, and a narrow pulse pressure fits a low stroke volume state such as severe aortic stenosis instead.

cards.q: A patient with a loud systolic murmur at the apex has a total left ventricular stroke volume of 90 mL, but only 55 mL reaches the aorta. What is the lesion, and what is the regurgitant volume?
cards.a: Mitral regurgitation, with 35 mL going backward into the left atrium.
options: Aortic regurgitation, with 35 mL returning from the aorta
Aortic stenosis, with 35 mL retained in the ventricle
Mitral regurgitation, with 55 mL going backward into the left atrium
Mitral regurgitation, with 35 mL going backward into the left atrium
cards.explanation: The ventricle emptied 90 mL but the aorta received 55 mL, so 35 mL went somewhere else, and a systolic murmur at the apex points to a leaking mitral valve carrying that blood back into the atrium. Blood retained in the ventricle would not count as part of the 90 mL ejected, so the aortic stenosis option misuses the numbers. Calling 55 mL the regurgitant volume reverses the forward and backward shares. Aortic regurgitation is diastolic and would not produce a systolic murmur at the apex.

cards.q: A low pitched extra sound is heard just after the second heart sound in a patient with a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle. Which sound is it, and what does its timing tell you about the mechanism?
cards.a: A third heart sound, generated as rapid early filling decelerates against a dilated wall.
options: A fourth heart sound, generated by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricular wall
A systolic murmur, generated by turbulent ejection
A split second sound, generated by delayed pulmonic closure
A third heart sound, generated as rapid early filling decelerates against a dilated wall
cards.explanation: Just after the second sound is early diastole, which is when the AV valve opens and blood rushes in, so an extra sound there is a third heart sound, and a dilated volume overloaded ventricle is exactly the setting that makes it audible. A fourth sound is late diastolic, arriving just before the first sound with atrial contraction, so its timing does not fit. A split second sound occurs at the second sound itself rather than after it. A systolic murmur would fall between the first and second sounds.

cards.q: How is stroke volume calculated?
cards.a: End diastolic volume minus end systolic volume.
options: End diastolic volume minus end systolic volume
End systolic volume minus end diastolic volume
End diastolic volume divided by end systolic volume
End diastolic volume plus end systolic volume
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is simply how much smaller the ventricle got during ejection, so it is the volume at the end of filling minus the volume left at the end of contraction. Reversing the subtraction gives a negative number, which no ejected volume can be. Dividing the two gives a unitless ratio rather than a volume. Adding them describes no physiological quantity at all.

cards.q: How is ejection fraction calculated?
cards.a: Stroke volume divided by end diastolic volume.
options: Stroke volume divided by end systolic volume
End systolic volume divided by end diastolic volume
Stroke volume divided by end diastolic volume
Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate
cards.explanation: Ejection fraction asks what share of the filled ventricle was actually pumped out, so the ejected volume goes over the volume present before ejection began. Dividing by end systolic volume compares the ejected blood with the leftover instead, which is not the standard index. End systolic over end diastolic volume gives the fraction retained, the complement of ejection fraction. Stroke volume times heart rate is cardiac output.

cards.q: What does end systolic volume represent?
cards.a: The blood remaining in the ventricle after ejection.
options: The blood ejected during one beat
The blood returning to the ventricle each minute
The blood present at the end of filling
The blood remaining in the ventricle after ejection
cards.explanation: Ejection never empties the ventricle, and end systolic volume is the reserve left behind once the semilunar valve closes. The blood ejected in one beat is stroke volume. The volume present at the end of filling is end diastolic volume, the largest volume of the cycle. Blood returning per minute is venous return, a flow rather than a chamber volume.

cards.q: About how large is left ventricular end diastolic volume in a resting adult?
cards.a: About 120 mL.
options: About 50 mL
About 70 mL
About 250 mL
About 120 mL
cards.explanation: A resting adult ventricle holds roughly 120 mL when filling ends, which is the number the rest of the course builds on. About 50 mL is the typical end systolic volume, and about 70 mL is the typical stroke volume, so those two are the leftover and the ejected shares of that 120 mL. About 250 mL would describe a markedly dilated ventricle rather than a normal one.

cards.q: About how large is left ventricular end systolic volume in a resting adult?
cards.a: About 50 mL.
options: About 70 mL
About 120 mL
About 50 mL
About 10 mL
cards.explanation: Roughly 50 mL stays behind after a normal beat, which is why ejection fraction sits near sixty percent rather than near one hundred. About 120 mL is the volume before ejection, not after it. About 70 mL is the volume ejected. About 10 mL would mean the ventricle nearly emptied every beat, which a healthy heart does not do even during exercise.

cards.q: What is a typical resting stroke volume in an adult?
cards.a: About 70 mL per beat.
options: About 20 mL per beat
About 70 mL per beat
About 120 mL per beat
About 200 mL per beat
cards.explanation: A resting ventricle filled to about 120 mL and left with about 50 mL ejects roughly 70 mL, and this is the value that combines with heart rate to give the familiar resting cardiac output near 5 L/min. About 20 mL would be severely low output. About 120 mL is the end diastolic volume rather than the ejected portion. About 200 mL exceeds what the chamber holds at rest.

cards.q: What is the normal range for left ventricular ejection fraction at rest?
cards.a: About 55 to 70 percent.
options: About 55 to 70 percent
About 40 to 50 percent
About 25 to 40 percent
About 85 to 95 percent
cards.explanation: A healthy ventricle ejects a little more than half of what it holds, which fits an end diastolic volume near 120 mL and a stroke volume near 70 mL. Values of 25 to 40 percent describe clearly reduced systolic function. Values of 40 to 50 percent sit in the borderline zone below normal. Values of 85 to 95 percent would mean the ventricle nearly empties each beat, leaving no reserve volume.

cards.q: An ejection fraction is generally described as clearly reduced when it falls below what value?
cards.a: About 40 percent.
options: About 75 percent
About 65 percent
About 55 percent
About 40 percent
cards.explanation: Below roughly 40 percent the ventricle is retaining well over half its filled volume each beat, and this is the threshold used to describe clearly reduced systolic function. Values around 55 percent sit at the bottom of the normal range rather than below it. Values of 65 and 75 percent are within or above normal, so neither marks a reduction.

cards.q: End diastolic volume is 130 mL and end systolic volume is 60 mL. What is the stroke volume?
cards.a: 70 mL.
options: 190 mL
60 mL
70 mL
130 mL
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is 130 minus 60, which is 70 mL. The value 190 mL comes from adding the two volumes rather than subtracting. The value 60 mL is the end systolic volume itself, the blood that stayed behind. The value 130 mL is the end diastolic volume, which the ventricle held before it contracted.

cards.q: End diastolic volume is 130 mL and end systolic volume is 60 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
cards.a: About 54 percent.
options: About 46 percent
About 117 percent
About 54 percent
About 86 percent
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is 130 minus 60, or 70 mL, and 70 divided by 130 is about 0.54, so the ejection fraction is about 54 percent. About 46 percent is 60 divided by 130, the fraction retained rather than ejected. About 117 percent comes from dividing 70 by 60, which uses end systolic volume as the denominator. About 86 percent would come from dividing 60 by 70, which reverses the quantities.

cards.q: End diastolic volume is 150 mL and end systolic volume is 90 mL. What are the stroke volume and ejection fraction?
cards.a: 60 mL and 40 percent.
options: 60 mL and 60 percent
90 mL and 60 percent
60 mL and 40 percent
240 mL and 40 percent
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is 150 minus 90, or 60 mL, and 60 divided by 150 is 0.40, so ejection fraction is 40 percent, and note that this ventricle is enlarged with its fraction sitting at the reduced threshold. Reporting 60 percent uses the retained fraction, 90 over 150, by mistake. Reporting 90 mL as the stroke volume names the leftover volume instead of the ejected one. Reporting 240 mL adds the two volumes rather than subtracting them.

cards.q: A ventricle with an end diastolic volume of 160 mL ejects 80 mL. What are its end systolic volume and ejection fraction?
cards.a: 80 mL and 50 percent.
options: 240 mL and 50 percent
80 mL and 50 percent
80 mL and 100 percent
160 mL and 50 percent
cards.explanation: If 80 mL of a 160 mL filling volume left the chamber, 80 mL remains, so end systolic volume is 80 mL and the ejection fraction is 80 divided by 160, or 50 percent. The value 240 mL comes from adding the ejected volume to the filled volume, which double counts. Calling it 100 percent divides stroke volume by end systolic volume rather than end diastolic volume. Reporting 160 mL as end systolic volume ignores that any blood left at all.

cards.q: A ventricle has an end diastolic volume of 120 mL and an ejection fraction of 60 percent. What are its stroke volume and end systolic volume?
cards.a: 72 mL and 48 mL.
options: 72 mL and 48 mL
60 mL and 60 mL
48 mL and 72 mL
72 mL and 120 mL
cards.explanation: Sixty percent of 120 mL is 72 mL ejected, and the remaining forty percent, 48 mL, stays behind as end systolic volume. Splitting the volume evenly into 60 and 60 would require an ejection fraction of exactly 50 percent. Reversing the numbers to 48 and 72 assigns the ejected share to the leftover. Listing 120 mL as end systolic volume would mean nothing was ejected at all.

cards.q: End diastolic volume is 140 mL and end systolic volume is 56 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
cards.a: 60 percent.
options: 40 percent
60 percent
84 percent
50 percent
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is 140 minus 56, or 84 mL, and 84 divided by 140 is 0.60, so the ejection fraction is 60 percent. The value 40 percent is 56 divided by 140, the retained fraction. The value 84 percent mistakes the stroke volume in milliliters for a percentage. Fifty percent would require an end systolic volume of 70 mL rather than 56 mL.

cards.q: A report gives an ejection fraction of 35 percent. What does that number say about the ventricle?
cards.a: It ejects about a third of its filled volume each beat, showing reduced function.
options: It retains about a third of its filled volume each beat, which is entirely normal
It ejects about a third of its filled volume each beat, showing reduced function
It fills to about a third of its usual end diastolic volume
It ejects a normal stroke volume at a reduced heart rate
cards.explanation: Ejection fraction is the share of end diastolic volume that leaves, so 35 percent means roughly two thirds of the filled volume stays behind, well below the normal 55 to 70 percent and a sign of weakened contraction. Retaining a third would correspond to an ejection fraction near 65 percent, which is normal, and that reversal is the most common misreading. Ejection fraction says nothing directly about how full the ventricle got, only what share left. It also carries no information about heart rate.

cards.q: Patient A has an end diastolic volume of 200 mL and an end systolic volume of 140 mL. A healthy control has 120 mL and 50 mL. Compare their stroke volumes and ejection fractions.
cards.a: A ejects 60 mL at 30 percent, the control ejects 70 mL at about 58 percent.
options: A ejects 60 mL at 30 percent, and both patients have the same ejection fraction
A ejects 60 mL at 58 percent, the control ejects 70 mL at 30 percent
A ejects 140 mL at 70 percent, the control ejects 50 mL at about 42 percent
A ejects 60 mL at 30 percent, the control ejects 70 mL at about 58 percent
cards.explanation: For A, 200 minus 140 is 60 mL, and 60 divided by 200 is 0.30. For the control, 120 minus 50 is 70 mL, and 70 divided by 120 is about 0.58. The dilated ventricle nearly keeps up on volume ejected by working from a much larger starting volume, but it does so at a far lower fraction, which is why ejection fraction detects the weakness that stroke volume alone can hide. Swapping the fractions, using the retained volumes as stroke volumes, or calling the two fractions equal all ignore the arithmetic above.

cards.q: A dilated ventricle has an end diastolic volume of 250 mL and an ejection fraction of 28 percent. What are its stroke volume and end systolic volume?
cards.a: 70 mL and 180 mL.
options: 70 mL and 180 mL
180 mL and 70 mL
28 mL and 222 mL
70 mL and 250 mL
cards.explanation: Twenty eight percent of 250 mL is 70 mL ejected, and 250 minus 70 leaves 180 mL behind, so the stroke volume is normal even though the ejection fraction is severely low, because the ventricle enlarged to compensate. Reversing to 180 and 70 assigns the retained volume to ejection. Treating 28 percent as 28 mL confuses a fraction with a volume. Listing 250 mL as end systolic volume ignores the 70 mL that left.

cards.q: A ventricle with an end diastolic volume of 120 mL normally leaves 50 mL behind. Contractility falls and end systolic volume rises to 75 mL with end diastolic volume unchanged on that beat. What are the new stroke volume and ejection fraction?
cards.a: 45 mL and about 38 percent.
options: 45 mL and about 62 percent
70 mL and about 58 percent
45 mL and about 38 percent
75 mL and about 63 percent
cards.explanation: Stroke volume becomes 120 minus 75, or 45 mL, and 45 divided by 120 is about 0.375, so the ejection fraction is about 38 percent, down from 70 mL and about 58 percent before. About 62 percent is the retained fraction, 75 over 120. The 70 mL and 58 percent pair describes the beat before contractility fell. Reporting 75 mL as the stroke volume names the blood that stayed behind.

cards.q: Two ventricles both have an ejection fraction of 55 percent, but one fills to 100 mL and the other to 160 mL. What does this show about ejection fraction as a measure?
cards.a: They eject 55 mL and 88 mL, so equal fractions can hide unequal outputs.
options: They eject 45 mL and 72 mL, the volumes retained in each ventricle
They eject the same stroke volume, because ejection fraction determines stroke volume by itself
They eject 55 mL and 88 mL, so equal fractions can hide unequal outputs
They eject 55 mL and 88 mL, so the second ventricle has better contractility
cards.explanation: Fifty five percent of 100 mL is 55 mL, while fifty five percent of 160 mL is 88 mL, so the fraction is a ratio and needs the filling volume before it tells you anything about output. Stroke volume cannot be read from the fraction alone, which is why calling the two outputs equal fails. The 45 and 72 mL figures are the retained volumes, the complement of what was ejected. A larger stroke volume here comes from greater filling at the same fraction, so it demonstrates preload rather than proving stronger contraction.

cards.q: How is cardiac output calculated?
cards.a: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
options: Heart rate divided by stroke volume
Stroke volume divided by end diastolic volume
Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
End diastolic volume minus end systolic volume
cards.explanation: Output per minute is how much leaves per beat multiplied by how many beats occur in that minute, so the two terms multiply. Dividing rate by stroke volume produces no meaningful unit. Stroke volume over end diastolic volume is ejection fraction. End diastolic minus end systolic volume is stroke volume itself, which is only one of the two factors cardiac output needs.

cards.q: What is a typical resting cardiac output for an adult?
cards.a: About 5 L/min.
options: About 5 L/min
About 1 L/min
About 15 L/min
About 25 L/min
cards.explanation: A resting rate near 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume near 70 mL give roughly 4.9 L/min, which is close to the whole blood volume circulating once each minute. About 1 L/min would not meet resting tissue demand. About 15 L/min is a moderate exercise value. About 25 L/min approaches the maximum a healthy young adult can reach, not a resting value.

cards.q: What is cardiac reserve?
cards.a: The difference between maximum cardiac output and resting cardiac output.
options: The blood left in the ventricle after ejection
The volume of blood held in the venous system
The difference between maximum cardiac output and resting cardiac output
The difference between end diastolic volume and end systolic volume
cards.explanation: Cardiac reserve measures how much extra flow the heart can supply above what it is already delivering at rest, so it is a difference of two outputs. Blood left after ejection is end systolic volume. Blood held in the veins is the venous reservoir, which supports preload but is not a reserve of output. The difference between end diastolic and end systolic volume is stroke volume, a per beat quantity rather than a per minute one.

cards.q: Which two variables determine cardiac output?
cards.a: Heart rate and stroke volume.
options: Heart rate and stroke volume
Stroke volume and end systolic volume
Heart rate and ejection fraction
Preload and afterload only
cards.explanation: Cardiac output is defined as the product of beats per minute and volume per beat, so those two variables set it directly and everything else acts through them. Ejection fraction influences stroke volume but is a ratio, so multiplying it by heart rate does not yield a flow. End systolic volume is one input to stroke volume rather than an independent determinant. Preload and afterload matter, but they work by changing stroke volume, so they are one step removed.

cards.q: How does the output of the right ventricle compare with that of the left ventricle over time?
cards.a: They are equal, because the two circuits are in series.
options: The right is about one fifth of the left
The right varies independently of the left from minute to minute
The right is about twice the left
They are equal, because the two circuits are in series
cards.explanation: Blood leaving the right ventricle must pass through the lungs and return to the left, so over any span of beats the two outputs have to match or blood would pile up in one circuit. The right ventricle generates about one fifth the pressure of the left, and that is the number students often transfer to output by mistake. Neither ventricle can sustain double the other's flow, and independent variation would flood the lungs within minutes.

cards.q: In a healthy young adult, maximum cardiac output is about how many times the resting value?
cards.a: About four to five times.
options: About one and a half times
About four to five times
About twenty times
About the same, since output cannot rise much
cards.explanation: Resting output near 5 L/min can climb to roughly 20 to 25 L/min in a healthy untrained adult, a fourfold to fivefold rise achieved by increasing both rate and stroke volume. A rise of only one and a half times would not support hard exercise. A twentyfold rise would demand an output near 100 L/min, which the circulation cannot carry. Output clearly does rise with demand, so claiming it cannot contradicts the existence of cardiac reserve.

cards.q: What is cardiac index?
cards.a: Cardiac output divided by body surface area.
options: Cardiac output divided by body surface area
Cardiac output divided by heart rate
Cardiac output multiplied by mean arterial pressure
Cardiac output divided by stroke volume
cards.explanation: Dividing output by body surface area scales the number to body size, so a small adult and a large adult can be compared fairly. Dividing output by heart rate simply returns stroke volume. Output times mean arterial pressure estimates the work the heart performs, not an index of flow. Output divided by stroke volume returns heart rate.

cards.q: Cardiac output is normally expressed in which units?
cards.a: Liters per minute.
options: Liters per minute
Milliliters per beat
Milliliters per liter
Millimeters of mercury
cards.explanation: Cardiac output is a flow, so it needs a volume over a time, and physiology reports it in liters per minute. Milliliters per beat is the unit of stroke volume, the per beat quantity that output is built from. Milliliters per liter is a ratio with no time in it. Millimeters of mercury measures pressure rather than flow.

cards.q: Heart rate is 72 beats per minute and stroke volume is 70 mL. What is the cardiac output?
cards.a: About 5.0 L/min.
options: About 0.5 L/min
About 5.0 L/min
About 50 L/min
About 1.0 L/min
cards.explanation: Multiplying 72 by 70 mL gives 5040 mL/min, which is 5.04 L/min once you divide by 1000. The other three answers each miss by a factor of ten or more, which usually comes from mishandling the conversion between milliliters and liters. Checking that the result lands near the familiar resting value of 5 L/min is a quick way to catch that error.

cards.q: Heart rate is 60 beats per minute and stroke volume is 80 mL. What is the cardiac output?
cards.a: 4.8 L/min.
options: 1.3 L/min
6.8 L/min
4.8 L/min
48 L/min
cards.explanation: Sixty beats times 80 mL is 4800 mL/min, or 4.8 L/min. The value 6.8 L/min comes from adding the two numbers instead of multiplying them. The value 1.3 L/min comes from dividing 80 by 60. The value 48 L/min misplaces the decimal by a factor of ten in the milliliter to liter conversion.

cards.q: During exercise, heart rate is 150 beats per minute and stroke volume is 100 mL. What is the cardiac output?
cards.a: 15 L/min.
options: 1.5 L/min
25 L/min
150 L/min
15 L/min
cards.explanation: Multiplying 150 by 100 mL gives 15000 mL/min, which is 15 L/min, about three times the resting value and a reasonable moderate exercise number. The value 1.5 L/min is off by a factor of ten and would be incompatible with life during exercise. The value 25 L/min comes from adding the two figures. The value 150 L/min skips the milliliter to liter conversion entirely.

cards.q: Cardiac output is 6.0 L/min and heart rate is 75 beats per minute. What is the stroke volume?
cards.a: 80 mL.
options: 45 mL
450 mL
125 mL
80 mL
cards.explanation: Rearranging the equation, stroke volume is cardiac output divided by heart rate, so 6000 mL/min divided by 75 beats per minute is 80 mL per beat. The value 125 mL comes from dividing 75 into 1000 by mistake rather than into the full output. The values 45 mL and 450 mL do not follow from either operation and are off by a factor of ten from each other, which is a sign that the unit conversion went astray.

cards.q: Cardiac output is 4.5 L/min and stroke volume is 75 mL. What is the heart rate?
cards.a: 60 beats per minute.
options: 45 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
90 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Heart rate is cardiac output divided by stroke volume, so 4500 mL/min divided by 75 mL per beat gives 60 beats per minute. The value 75 simply repeats the stroke volume as though it were the rate. The values 45 and 90 do not satisfy the equation, since 45 times 75 is 3375 mL/min and 90 times 75 is 6750 mL/min, neither of which is 4500 mL/min.

cards.q: A student has a resting cardiac output of 5 L/min and a maximum cardiac output of 25 L/min. What is the cardiac reserve?
cards.a: 20 L/min.
options: 5 L/min
25 L/min
20 L/min
30 L/min
cards.explanation: Cardiac reserve is the maximum minus the resting output, so 25 minus 5 is 20 L/min of extra flow available on demand. The value 25 L/min is the maximum itself, which counts the resting output as though it were reserve. The value 5 L/min is the resting output. The value 30 L/min adds the two rather than subtracting.

cards.q: Heart rate doubles from 70 to 140 beats per minute while stroke volume stays at 70 mL. What happens to cardiac output?
cards.a: It doubles, from about 4.9 to about 9.8 L/min.
options: It rises by half, from about 4.9 to about 7.4 L/min
It stays near 4.9 L/min because stroke volume did not change
It doubles, from about 4.9 to about 9.8 L/min
It quadruples, from about 4.9 to about 19.6 L/min
cards.explanation: Output is the product of the two terms, so doubling one while holding the other constant doubles the product: 70 times 70 mL is 4900 mL/min and 140 times 70 mL is 9800 mL/min. A rise of half would require a rate near 105, and output cannot hold steady when one of its two factors doubles. Quadrupling would require both terms to double, not just the rate. In a real heart this fast, filling time would shorten and stroke volume would not hold perfectly constant.

cards.q: Heart rate rises from 70 to 180 beats per minute, and because filling time is cut, stroke volume falls from 70 to 50 mL. Calculate cardiac output before and after and state the net effect.
cards.a: 4.9 L/min before and 9.0 L/min after, so output still rises.
options: 4.9 L/min before and 3.5 L/min after, so output falls
4.9 L/min before and 9.0 L/min after, so output still rises
4.9 L/min before and 12.6 L/min after, so output rises more than twofold
4.9 L/min before and 4.9 L/min after, so output is unchanged
cards.explanation: Before, 70 times 70 mL is 4900 mL/min, and after, 180 times 50 mL is 9000 mL/min. The fall in stroke volume blunts the gain but does not erase it, because the rate rose proportionally more than the volume per beat fell. Output falling would require the stroke volume to drop below about 27 mL, and it cannot be unchanged when both factors moved by different proportions. The 12.6 L/min figure keeps stroke volume at 70 mL and ignores the shortened filling time.

cards.q: A trained athlete has a resting heart rate of 50 beats per minute with a stroke volume of 100 mL, and at peak exercise reaches 190 beats per minute with a stroke volume of 160 mL. What are the resting output, the maximum output, and the cardiac reserve?
cards.a: 5.0 L/min, 30.4 L/min, and a reserve of 25.4 L/min.
options: 5.0 L/min, 30.4 L/min, and a reserve of 25.4 L/min
5.0 L/min, 30.4 L/min, and a reserve of 35.4 L/min
5.0 L/min, 19.0 L/min, and a reserve of 14.0 L/min
8.0 L/min, 30.4 L/min, and a reserve of 22.4 L/min
cards.explanation: At rest, 50 times 100 mL is 5000 mL/min, or 5.0 L/min, a normal resting output achieved with a slow rate and a large stroke volume. At peak, 190 times 160 mL is 30400 mL/min, or 30.4 L/min, and the reserve is 30.4 minus 5.0, which is 25.4 L/min. Adding the two outputs gives 35.4 and misdefines reserve, while the 19.0 L/min figure holds stroke volume at its resting value. The 8.0 L/min resting figure does not follow from 50 times 100 mL.

cards.q: A patient in heart failure maintains a resting cardiac output of 4.0 L/min with a heart rate of 100 and a stroke volume of 40 mL, and can reach only 8.0 L/min at maximum. Compare the cardiac reserve with the healthy value of about 20 L/min and explain the consequence.
cards.a: The reserve is 4.0 L/min, a fifth of normal, so ordinary activity exhausts it.
options: The reserve is 8.0 L/min, half of normal, so only strenuous exercise is limited
The reserve is 4.0 L/min, a fifth of normal, so ordinary activity exhausts it
The reserve is 12.0 L/min, close to normal, so exercise tolerance is preserved
The reserve is 4.0 L/min, but because resting output is normal, exercise capacity is unaffected
cards.explanation: Reserve is maximum minus resting output, so 8.0 minus 4.0 leaves 4.0 L/min, compared with about 20 L/min in a healthy adult. Because even light activity calls for several liters per minute of extra flow, that small margin is used up quickly, which is why fatigue appears at low workloads. Calling the reserve 8.0 L/min mistakes the maximum for the margin above rest, and no arithmetic here yields 12.0 L/min. Resting output being adequate does not protect exercise capacity, since it is the margin above rest that exercise draws on.

cards.q: Compare a heart at 200 beats per minute with a stroke volume of 35 mL against the same heart at 150 beats per minute with a stroke volume of 60 mL. Which produces more cardiac output, and what principle does the comparison illustrate?
cards.a: The slower rate gives 9.0 L/min against 7.0 L/min, so extra rate costs filling.
options: The slower rate gives 9.0 L/min against 7.0 L/min, so extra rate costs filling
The faster rate gives 9.0 L/min against 7.0 L/min, showing that rate always dominates output
Both give 7.0 L/min, showing that rate and stroke volume always trade off exactly
The faster rate gives 7.0 L/min against 6.0 L/min, showing that faster is always better
cards.explanation: At 200 beats per minute, 200 times 35 mL is 7000 mL/min, and at 150 beats per minute, 150 times 60 mL is 9000 mL/min, so the slower heart moves more blood. The reason is that diastole is where filling happens, and once the rate is high enough to squeeze filling severely, each added beat carries too little volume to pay for itself. The trade off is not exact, as these numbers show, and rate does not always dominate, which is precisely the point of the comparison.

cards.q: What does the Frank Starling law of the heart state?
cards.a: The greater the end diastolic volume, the greater the force of the next contraction.
options: The greater the arterial pressure, the greater the force of the next contraction
The greater the end diastolic volume, the greater the force of the next contraction
The faster the heart rate, the greater the force of each contraction
The greater the sympathetic input, the greater the force of the next contraction
cards.explanation: The law connects filling to force: a ventricle stretched more by the blood returning to it contracts harder on the next beat, within limits, which is how the heart matches its output to its input beat by beat. Arterial pressure is afterload, which opposes ejection rather than driving the length dependent increase in force. A faster rate does modestly increase force through calcium accumulation, but that is a separate effect and not what Frank Starling describes. Sympathetic input raises contractility, which shifts the whole relationship rather than acting through length.

cards.q: On a Frank Starling curve, what is plotted on the horizontal axis?
cards.a: End diastolic volume, an index of preload.
options: End diastolic volume, an index of preload
Aortic pressure, an index of afterload
Heart rate
Ejection fraction
cards.explanation: The curve asks how filling determines performance, so the input variable on the horizontal axis is the volume the ventricle holds when contraction begins. Aortic pressure is afterload, which shifts the curve rather than serving as its axis. Heart rate is not part of this relationship, which describes a single beat. Ejection fraction is a derived ratio and is not the standard axis.

cards.q: On a Frank Starling curve, what is plotted on the vertical axis?
cards.a: Stroke volume, or stroke work.
options: End systolic volume
Venous return
Stroke volume, or stroke work
Mean arterial pressure
cards.explanation: The output of the relationship is how much the ventricle accomplishes on that beat, expressed as the volume ejected or the work performed. End systolic volume is the leftover rather than the performance measure. Venous return is upstream of the curve and acts by setting the horizontal position. Mean arterial pressure depends on the whole circulation, not on the single beat this curve describes.

cards.q: What is the main cellular basis of the Frank Starling relationship?
cards.a: Stretching the sarcomere improves filament overlap and raises troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+.
options: Stretch increases the number of myocytes recruited for the contraction
Stretch opens voltage gated Na+ channels and lengthens the cardiac action potential
Stretching the sarcomere improves filament overlap and raises troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+
Stretch raises the resting membrane potential and speeds conduction
cards.explanation: Lengthening the sarcomere toward its optimum both improves the geometry of cross bridge formation and, importantly, makes the thin filament respond more strongly to the same Ca2+ transient, so force rises without any change in Ca2+ release. Stretch does not act by changing Na+ channel gating or action potential duration. Recruitment of additional cells is a skeletal muscle strategy and is impossible in the heart, where the whole syncytium contracts together each beat. Conduction speed governs the timing of activation, not the force it produces.

cards.q: Which two factors most directly determine end diastolic volume?
cards.a: Venous return and the time available for filling.
options: Venous return and the time available for filling
Aortic pressure and arteriolar resistance
Contractility and end systolic volume
Ejection fraction and heart rate
cards.explanation: How full the ventricle gets depends on how much blood arrives and how long the AV valve is open to admit it, so venous return and diastolic duration set end diastolic volume. Aortic pressure and arteriolar resistance act on the ejection side as afterload. Contractility and end systolic volume influence how much blood is left over to add to the next filling but do not set the filling itself. Ejection fraction is a result of the beat rather than a determinant of filling.
