cards.q: At what sarcomere length does cardiac muscle generate maximum force?
cards.a: About 2.2 micrometers.
options: About 1.2 micrometers
About 3.6 micrometers
About 2.2 micrometers
About 0.8 micrometers
cards.explanation: Optimal overlap of thick and thin filaments occurs near 2.2 micrometers, and the resting cardiac sarcomere sits below this length, which is why extra filling increases force. About 1.2 micrometers would be an overly shortened sarcomere with filaments colliding. About 3.6 micrometers is beyond the range where overlap exists and would generate almost no force. About 0.8 micrometers is shorter than a sarcomere gets in a working heart.

cards.q: Where on its length tension relationship does the normal heart operate at rest?
cards.a: On the ascending limb, below optimal sarcomere length.
options: On the descending limb, beyond optimal length
At the exact peak of the curve
On the ascending limb, below optimal sarcomere length
Off the curve entirely, since length does not affect cardiac force
cards.explanation: Resting cardiac sarcomeres are shorter than optimal, which leaves room for extra filling to increase force and is what makes the Frank Starling mechanism useful. Sitting at the peak would leave no headroom for stretch to help. The stiff collagen network around cardiac muscle largely prevents it from reaching the descending limb, which is one difference from skeletal muscle. Length clearly does affect cardiac force, which is the whole premise of the relationship.

cards.q: Which mechanism keeps right ventricular output matched to left ventricular output beat by beat?
cards.a: The Frank Starling relationship.
options: Vagal tone at the SA node
The intrinsic rhythm of the AV node
The baroreceptor reflex
The Frank Starling relationship
cards.explanation: If one ventricle pumps slightly more, the extra blood arrives at the other ventricle, stretches it, and makes it eject more on the following beats, so the mismatch corrects itself without any nerves involved. Vagal tone sets heart rate, which is identical for both ventricles and therefore cannot balance their stroke volumes. The baroreceptor reflex regulates arterial pressure over seconds and is far too slow and too global for beat by beat matching. The AV node governs conduction timing, not ejected volume.

cards.q: Venous return increases while heart rate and contractility are held constant. Predict end diastolic volume and stroke volume.
cards.a: End diastolic volume rises and stroke volume rises.
options: End diastolic volume rises and stroke volume rises
End diastolic volume rises and stroke volume falls
End diastolic volume falls and stroke volume rises
Both are unchanged, because contractility did not change
cards.explanation: More blood returning fills the ventricle further, and the extra stretch produces a stronger contraction, so both quantities rise together. Stroke volume cannot fall on greater filling unless something also opposed ejection. End diastolic volume cannot fall when more blood is arriving. Contractility is not the only route to a larger stroke volume, and treating it as such is exactly the confusion the Frank Starling mechanism resolves.

cards.q: A patient loses a liter of blood. Using the Frank Starling relationship alone, predict what happens to stroke volume.
cards.a: It falls, because reduced venous return lowers end diastolic volume and stretch.
options: It rises, because the heart compensates by contracting harder
It falls, because afterload has increased
It is unchanged, because the ventricle always ejects the same fraction
It falls, because reduced venous return lowers end diastolic volume and stretch
cards.explanation: Less blood in the system means less returning to the heart, so the ventricle fills less, the sarcomeres are stretched less, and the next contraction is weaker. Reflex sympathetic activity does raise contractility after hemorrhage, but that is a separate mechanism and not what the Frank Starling relationship alone predicts. Ejecting a constant fraction would still mean a smaller volume ejected from a smaller filled volume. Afterload actually tends to fall as arterial pressure drops, so it is not the cause here.

cards.q: A student stands up quickly and blood pools in the leg veins. Before any reflex responds, what happens to stroke volume?
cards.a: It falls, because less blood returns to fill the ventricle.
options: It rises, because gravity assists ejection
It is unchanged, because total blood volume did not change
It falls, because less blood returns to fill the ventricle
It rises, because heart rate increases immediately
cards.explanation: Pooling traps blood in the compliant leg veins, so venous return drops, end diastolic volume falls, and the less stretched ventricle ejects less on the next beat. Gravity does not assist ejection from the left ventricle in any meaningful way. Total blood volume is indeed unchanged, but its distribution is what matters for filling, and that is the point students often miss. The reflex rise in heart rate comes afterward and is a response to the fall in output rather than a cause of a rise.

cards.q: The heart rate slows from 80 to 55 beats per minute with venous return unchanged. Predict end diastolic volume and stroke volume.
cards.a: Both rise, because longer diastole allows more filling.
options: Both rise, because longer diastole allows more filling
Both fall, because fewer beats deliver less blood
End diastolic volume rises but stroke volume falls
Both are unchanged, because venous return did not change
cards.explanation: A slower rate lengthens diastole, the AV valve stays open longer, more blood accumulates in the ventricle, and the extra stretch produces a bigger ejection. Fewer beats per minute does lower cardiac output if stroke volume did not compensate, but that is a per minute statement rather than a per beat one. Stroke volume cannot fall while stretch increases, unless afterload also rose. Unchanged venous return per minute is precisely why the extra time concentrates more blood into each beat.

cards.q: Does an increase in end diastolic volume alone change contractility?
cards.a: No, it moves the ventricle along the same curve without changing the curve itself.
options: Yes, because more stretch means stronger contraction, which is contractility
No, it moves the ventricle along the same curve without changing the curve itself
Yes, because Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum increases with stretch
No, because stretch has no effect on the force of contraction
cards.explanation: Contractility is defined as the force generated at a given fiber length, so a change that works by altering length is by definition not a change in contractility, and the ventricle simply operates at a new point on the same relationship. Calling extra stretch contractility is the most common error here, and it matters because contractility changes shift the entire curve. Stretch increases the responsiveness of the filaments to Ca2+ rather than increasing the amount of Ca2+ released. Stretch certainly does increase force, so denying any effect of length contradicts the law itself.

cards.q: The right ventricle transiently ejects more than the left. What happens over the next several beats?
cards.a: Left ventricular filling rises, stretching it more, so left stroke volume rises to match.
options: Left ventricular filling falls, so left stroke volume falls further behind
Left ventricular filling rises, stretching it more, so left stroke volume rises to match
The right ventricle slows its rate until the two match
Blood accumulates in the lungs permanently, since nothing corrects the imbalance
cards.explanation: Extra blood pumped by the right ventricle crosses the lungs and arrives at the left atrium, filling the left ventricle more, and the added stretch raises left stroke volume until the outputs are equal again. Left filling rises rather than falls, because the extra volume has nowhere else to go. The two ventricles share the same rate, so the right cannot slow independently. The imbalance does correct itself, which is why a modest mismatch does not flood the lungs.

cards.q: Increasing sarcomere length raises force at the same intracellular Ca2+ level. Which change explains this?
cards.a: Increased sensitivity of troponin C to Ca2+ along with better filament overlap.
options: Increased sensitivity of troponin C to Ca2+ along with better filament overlap
A larger Ca2+ transient released per action potential
Recruitment of additional motor units within the ventricular wall syncytium
A longer action potential plateau at greater lengths
cards.explanation: The question specifies the same Ca2+ level, so the extra force must come from the filaments using that Ca2+ more effectively, which is the length dependent rise in troponin C sensitivity combined with improved cross bridge geometry. A larger Ca2+ transient would contradict the stated condition. Motor unit recruitment does not exist in cardiac muscle, since the myocardium contracts as one functional unit. A longer plateau would change Ca2+ entry, which again the question has held fixed.

cards.q: One intervention raises venous return, and another delivers norepinephrine to the ventricle. Both raise stroke volume. How do their effects differ on the Frank Starling curve?
cards.a: Venous return moves the ventricle along the curve, while norepinephrine shifts the curve.
options: Both move the ventricle rightward along the same curve
Both shift the curve upward, since both increase force
Venous return shifts the curve upward, while norepinephrine moves the ventricle along it
Venous return moves the ventricle along the curve, while norepinephrine shifts the curve
cards.explanation: Extra filling changes only the starting length, so the ventricle relocates to a new point on the existing relationship. Norepinephrine changes how much force the muscle makes at any given length, so it lifts the entire relationship and produces a larger stroke volume even at the original end diastolic volume. Treating both as movement along one curve erases the concept of contractility. Swapping the two mechanisms reverses their meanings, and calling both a shift of the curve ignores that only one acts independently of length.

cards.q: A patient is placed on positive pressure ventilation, which raises intrathoracic pressure throughout the respiratory cycle. Trace the effect on venous return, end diastolic volume, and stroke volume.
cards.a: Venous return falls, end diastolic volume falls, and stroke volume falls.
options: Venous return rises, end diastolic volume rises, and stroke volume rises
Venous return is unchanged, but stroke volume falls from increased afterload
Venous return falls, end diastolic volume rises, and stroke volume rises
Venous return falls, end diastolic volume falls, and stroke volume falls
cards.explanation: Blood returns to the chest because thoracic pressure is normally lower than pressure in the abdomen and limbs, so raising thoracic pressure narrows that gradient and slows return. Less blood arriving means less filling, and less stretch means a weaker ejection, so all three fall in sequence. Return cannot rise when the pressure gradient driving it is reduced, and filling cannot rise while return falls. Left ventricular afterload is actually reduced somewhat by raised thoracic pressure, so blaming increased afterload names the wrong mechanism.

cards.q: After a hemorrhage, a patient's stroke volume is low. A transfusion restores blood volume. Explain the recovery in terms of the curve, and state whether contractility changed.
cards.a: Restored venous return moves the ventricle back along the same curve, with contractility unchanged.
options: The transfusion raises contractility directly, shifting the curve upward
Restored venous return moves the ventricle back along the same curve, with contractility unchanged
The transfusion lowers afterload, which is what restores stroke volume
End systolic volume falls, which is what raises stroke volume, and contractility has risen
cards.explanation: Adding volume acts on filling, so it restores the stretch that was lost and the ventricle returns to its earlier operating point on an unchanged relationship. Contractility describes force at a fixed length and is not altered by volume itself. A transfusion tends to raise arterial pressure rather than lower afterload. Stroke volume here recovers because end diastolic volume rose, not because end systolic volume fell, which is the signature of a genuine contractility change.

cards.q: A patient with a dilated failing ventricle is already operating on the flat part of a depressed Frank Starling curve. Additional intravenous fluid is given. Predict the effect on stroke volume and on filling pressure.
cards.a: Stroke volume increases little, while filling pressure rises substantially.
options: Both stroke volume and filling pressure fall
Stroke volume rises steeply, as it would in a normal heart
Stroke volume increases little, while filling pressure rises substantially
Stroke volume rises and filling pressure falls, because the ventricle empties better
cards.explanation: On the flat portion of the curve, further stretch buys almost no additional force, so the added volume mostly raises the pressure in the ventricle and upstream in the atrium and pulmonary veins rather than the volume ejected. A steep rise in stroke volume is what a normal heart on the ascending limb would show, and confusing the two is why volume loading can help one patient and congest another. Adding fluid cannot lower filling pressure or stroke volume. Better emptying would require a contractility change, which fluid does not provide.

cards.q: What is preload?
cards.a: The stretch on the wall at the end of filling, indexed by end diastolic volume.
options: The stretch on the wall at the end of filling, indexed by end diastolic volume
The pressure the ventricle must exceed to open the semilunar valve and eject
The force the muscle generates at any given fiber length
The volume of blood left in the ventricle after ejection
cards.explanation: Preload is the load placed on the muscle before it contracts, which in the intact ventricle is the stretch produced by the blood it has taken in, so end diastolic volume is its practical index. The pressure that must be exceeded to eject is afterload, the load encountered after contraction begins. Force at a given length is contractility. The volume left after ejection is end systolic volume, which is a result of the beat rather than the load that set it up.

cards.q: What is afterload?
cards.a: The load the ventricle must overcome to eject, indexed by arterial pressure.
options: The load the ventricle must overcome to eject, indexed by arterial pressure
The stretch on the ventricular wall at the end of diastole
The intrinsic strength of the muscle at any fixed fiber length
The volume of blood returning to the heart from the veins each minute
cards.explanation: Afterload is what opposes shortening once contraction has started, and since the semilunar valve will not open until ventricular pressure passes arterial pressure, aortic pressure is the usual index. End diastolic stretch is preload, the load present before contraction. Intrinsic strength at a fixed length is contractility. Blood returning per minute is venous return, which sets preload rather than opposing ejection.

cards.q: What is contractility?
cards.a: The force developed at a given fiber length, independent of loading.
options: The amount the ventricular wall is stretched before it contracts
The pressure in the aorta that the ventricle must eject against
The total volume the ventricle ejects during a single beat
The force developed at a given fiber length, independent of loading
cards.explanation: Contractility is defined by holding length constant and asking how strong the beat is, which is why it is often called the inotropic state and why it is changed by things like norepinephrine that alter calcium handling rather than filling. Stretch before contraction is preload, and aortic pressure during ejection is afterload, and both are loads rather than properties of the muscle. Volume ejected per beat is stroke volume, which all three of these variables help determine and so cannot define any one of them.

cards.q: Which variable is most directly changed by an increase in venous return?
cards.a: Preload.
options: Afterload
Contractility
Preload
Heart rate
cards.explanation: Venous return determines how much blood reaches the ventricle before it contracts, so it acts on the filling side and sets preload. Afterload is set on the arterial side by pressure and resistance. Contractility is set by calcium handling within the myocyte and is unaffected by how full the chamber is. Heart rate is governed by the SA node and autonomic input, not by the volume returning, although stretch of the atria can nudge it modestly.

cards.q: Which variable is most directly changed by widespread arteriolar constriction?
cards.a: Afterload.
options: Preload
Afterload
Contractility
Ejection fraction
cards.explanation: Constricting arterioles raises systemic resistance and therefore arterial pressure, which is exactly the load the ventricle must overcome to open the aortic valve and eject. Preload is set by venous filling, and while arteriolar tone eventually influences it, the direct effect is on the arterial side. Contractility is a property of the myocyte and is unchanged by vessel tone. Ejection fraction is a downstream result of the load change, not the variable being altered.

cards.q: Which variable is most directly changed when norepinephrine binds beta1 receptors on ventricular myocytes?
cards.a: Contractility.
options: Preload
Contractility
Afterload
Ventricular compliance during filling
cards.explanation: Beta1 activation raises cAMP and PKA activity, which phosphorylates L type Ca2+ channels and phospholamban so more Ca2+ is available per beat, and that is a change in force at any given length, which is contractility. Preload would require a change in filling, and afterload a change in arterial load, neither of which follows from a receptor on the ventricular myocyte. Relaxation does speed up with PKA activity, but the defining effect measured here is the increase in force.

cards.q: The slope of the end systolic pressure volume relationship is an index of which variable?
cards.a: Contractility.
options: Preload
Contractility
Venous return
Afterload
cards.explanation: That line is drawn through the points where ejection stops across many different loading conditions, so its slope reports the strength of the muscle itself rather than the conditions it worked under. Preload is read as a position on the volume axis at the end of filling. Afterload is read as the pressure at which ejection begins. Venous return acts on preload and is upstream of the ventricle entirely.

cards.q: Which of these is plotted on the horizontal axis of a Frank Starling curve?
cards.a: Preload.
options: Preload
Contractility
Afterload
Stroke work
cards.explanation: The Frank Starling relationship describes how filling determines performance, so the input variable is preload, usually expressed as end diastolic volume. Contractility is not an axis but rather determines which curve you are on, since a rise in contractility lifts the whole curve. Afterload also shifts the curve rather than serving as an axis. Stroke work is a possible vertical axis, the output of the relationship, not the input.

cards.q: Preload increases while afterload and contractility are held constant. What happens to stroke volume?
cards.a: It rises, because greater stretch produces a stronger contraction.
options: It rises, because greater stretch produces a stronger contraction
It falls, because the ventricle is overfilled
It is unchanged, because contractility did not change
It rises, because afterload falls when the ventricle is fuller
cards.explanation: More filling stretches the sarcomeres closer to their optimal length and raises troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+, so the ventricle ejects more without any change in its contractile state. Overfilling only reduces output in a failing or extremely dilated ventricle, not within the normal working range. Assuming stroke volume can only rise if contractility rises is the error this card targets. Afterload was specified as constant, so it cannot be the explanation.

cards.q: Afterload increases while preload and contractility are held constant. What happens to stroke volume and end systolic volume on that beat?
cards.a: Stroke volume falls and end systolic volume rises.
options: Stroke volume rises and end systolic volume falls
Both fall
Stroke volume falls and end systolic volume rises
Both rise
cards.explanation: A higher pressure to eject against means the ventricle shortens less before the valve closes, so less blood leaves and more stays behind. Since preload is fixed, whatever is not ejected must remain, so the two move in opposite directions. Both falling would require blood to disappear from the chamber, and both rising would require more blood to be present than the fixed end diastolic volume allows. A rise in stroke volume with a smaller residual is the contractility response, which is the confusion worth guarding against here.

cards.q: Contractility increases while preload and afterload are held constant. What happens to stroke volume and end systolic volume?
cards.a: Stroke volume rises and end systolic volume falls.
options: Stroke volume rises and end systolic volume rises
Stroke volume rises and end diastolic volume rises
Stroke volume is unchanged and end systolic volume falls
Stroke volume rises and end systolic volume falls
cards.explanation: A stronger beat empties the ventricle further at the same load, so less blood remains and more is ejected, which is the fingerprint that separates a contractility change from a preload change. End systolic volume cannot rise when the muscle contracts more forcefully at the same load. End diastolic volume was held constant, so it cannot be the source of the extra output. Stroke volume must change if end systolic volume falls at a fixed end diastolic volume, since the two differ by exactly that amount.

cards.q: A patient receives a rapid intravenous infusion of saline. Which variable rises first?
cards.a: Preload.
options: Contractility
Ejection fraction
Afterload
Preload
cards.explanation: Extra fluid expands blood volume, raises venous return, and fills the ventricle more, which is a preload increase. Contractility is unchanged because nothing has altered myocyte calcium handling. Arterial pressure may rise a little as output increases, so afterload is a later and secondary effect. Ejection fraction may change slightly but is a computed ratio rather than a variable an infusion acts on directly.

cards.q: Aortic valve stenosis narrows the outflow orifice. Which variable does it primarily increase?
cards.a: Afterload.
options: Preload
Contractility
Venous return
Afterload
cards.explanation: A narrowed valve means the ventricle must generate a much higher pressure than the aorta itself carries in order to push blood through, which is a large increase in the load opposing ejection. Preload may rise later as end systolic volume accumulates, but the primary lesion is on the ejection side. Contractility is a myocyte property and is not changed by the valve. Venous return is set by the systemic circulation upstream, not by the outflow valve.

cards.q: A vasodilator lowers systemic arterial pressure. Predict the effect on afterload and on stroke volume.
cards.a: Afterload falls and stroke volume rises.
options: Afterload rises and stroke volume falls
Afterload falls and stroke volume falls
Afterload falls and stroke volume rises
Afterload is unchanged and stroke volume rises
cards.explanation: Less arterial pressure means the aortic valve opens sooner and the ventricle can keep shortening for longer before the pressure gradient reverses, so more blood is ejected. Afterload cannot rise when the pressure that defines it has fallen. Stroke volume falling would require the ventricle to be more opposed, not less. Arterial pressure is the main index of afterload, so it cannot be unchanged when that pressure drops.

cards.q: A beta1 receptor blocker is given. Which variable falls, and what happens to stroke volume at a fixed preload and afterload?
cards.a: Contractility falls, so stroke volume falls.
options: Contractility falls, so stroke volume falls
Afterload falls, so stroke volume rises
Preload falls, so stroke volume falls
Contractility falls, but stroke volume is unchanged
cards.explanation: Blocking beta1 receptors removes the sympathetic drive that raises cAMP and calcium entry, so the ventricle generates less force at any given length and ejects less from the same filling volume. Preload is set by venous return and is not directly reduced by the block. Afterload is set by arterial vessels and is likewise not the primary target. Stroke volume must fall when force falls at fixed loading, which is what makes contractility an independent determinant.

cards.q: Arterial pressure is raised sharply and venous return is unchanged. Trace what happens to stroke volume, end systolic volume, and end diastolic volume over the next few beats.
cards.a: Stroke volume falls and end systolic volume rises, then end diastolic volume rises and stroke volume partly recovers.
options: End diastolic volume rises first, which then lowers end systolic volume and raises stroke volume above baseline
Stroke volume falls and end systolic volume falls at once, then end diastolic volume falls further
Stroke volume rises because the ventricle contracts harder against the higher pressure
Stroke volume falls and end systolic volume rises, then end diastolic volume rises and stroke volume partly recovers
cards.explanation: The immediate effect of more afterload is incomplete ejection, so end systolic volume rises and stroke volume falls on that beat. That leftover blood then adds to an unchanged venous return, so end diastolic volume rises, the extra stretch strengthens the next contractions, and stroke volume climbs partway back. End systolic volume cannot fall when ejection is more opposed, and end diastolic volume rises as a consequence of the poor emptying rather than before it. The ventricle does not raise its own contractility in response to pressure, which is the key distinction between a load and an inotropic change.

cards.q: Two interventions each raise stroke volume from 70 to 90 mL in the same patient: a fluid bolus and an infusion that raises contractility. Which measurement distinguishes them?
cards.a: End systolic volume falls with the contractility change but not with the fluid bolus.
options: End diastolic volume falls with the fluid bolus but rises with the contractility change
End systolic volume falls with the contractility change but not with the fluid bolus
Stroke volume is the only measurement that changes in either case
Ejection fraction falls in both cases because the ventricle works harder
cards.explanation: A fluid bolus works by filling the ventricle more, so end diastolic volume climbs while the ventricle still stops ejecting at roughly the same residual volume. A contractility increase works by emptying the ventricle further, so end systolic volume drops while filling is essentially unchanged, and that difference in which end of the beat moved is the cleanest distinction between preload and inotropy. Reversing the two, so that filling falls with fluid and rises with inotropy, gets both directions backward. Stroke volume alone cannot distinguish them, and ejection fraction rises in both cases rather than falling.

cards.q: A balloon is inflated in the vena cava, reducing the blood reaching the right atrium. Predict stroke volume and state whether contractility has changed.
cards.a: Stroke volume falls because preload fell, and contractility is unchanged.
options: Stroke volume falls because contractility fell, and preload is unchanged
Stroke volume falls because preload fell, and contractility is unchanged
Stroke volume falls because afterload rose, and contractility is unchanged
Stroke volume is unchanged, because contractility determines it
cards.explanation: Obstructing venous return starves the ventricle of filling, so end diastolic volume and sarcomere stretch fall and the next beat ejects less, all along the same Frank Starling curve. Nothing has touched myocyte calcium handling, so the muscle is exactly as strong as before at any given length, which is what contractility means. Afterload has not risen, and in fact arterial pressure will fall as output declines. Stroke volume depends on loading as well as contractility, so it cannot hold steady when filling collapses.

cards.q: A patient has a reduced stroke volume with an elevated end diastolic volume, an elevated end systolic volume, and a normal arterial pressure. Which variable has changed?
cards.a: Contractility has fallen.
options: Preload has fallen
Contractility has fallen
Afterload has risen
Preload has risen and is the cause of the reduced stroke volume
cards.explanation: Filling is generous and the arterial load is normal, yet the ventricle still leaves an unusually large residual and ejects less, so the weakness must be in the muscle itself, which is a fall in contractility. Preload has clearly not fallen, since end diastolic volume is elevated. Afterload has not risen, since arterial pressure is normal, and a rise there would be needed to explain poor emptying by load. The elevated preload is a consequence of poor emptying rather than the cause of the low output, and reading that arrow backward is the mistake this scenario is designed to catch.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter do sympathetic postganglionic fibers release onto the heart?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.
options: Acetylcholine
Glutamate
Dopamine
Norepinephrine
cards.explanation: Sympathetic postganglionic neurons supplying the SA node and myocardium release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors. Acetylcholine is released by the parasympathetic postganglionic fibers of the vagus, and also by sympathetic preganglionic fibers, which is why the word appears in both divisions and causes confusion. Dopamine acts mainly as a central transmitter and a circulating agent rather than the transmitter at these terminals. Glutamate is a central nervous system transmitter and has no role at cardiac neuroeffector junctions.

cards.q: Which receptor does norepinephrine act on in the heart?
cards.a: The beta1 adrenergic receptor.
options: The alpha1 adrenergic receptor
The beta2 adrenergic receptor
The muscarinic M2 receptor
The beta1 adrenergic receptor
cards.explanation: Cardiac pacemaker and contractile cells carry beta1 receptors, which is why beta1 selective drugs act on the heart with relatively little effect elsewhere. Alpha1 receptors dominate on vascular smooth muscle, where they cause constriction. Beta2 receptors are found mainly on bronchiolar and vascular smooth muscle, where they cause relaxation. The muscarinic M2 receptor is the cardiac receptor for the parasympathetic transmitter, not the sympathetic one.

cards.q: Which second messenger pathway does beta1 receptor activation use?
cards.a: Gs protein, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A.
options: Gq protein, phospholipase C, IP3, and diacylglycerol
Direct opening of a ligand gated Na+ channel
Gi protein, reduced adenylyl cyclase activity, and less cAMP
Gs protein, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A
cards.explanation: Beta1 receptors couple to Gs, which stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raises cAMP, and activates protein kinase A to phosphorylate the calcium handling proteins that speed and strengthen the beat. The Gq pathway with IP3 and diacylglycerol is what alpha1 receptors use on vascular smooth muscle. The Gi pathway that lowers cAMP is the muscarinic M2 pathway, the opposing arm in the heart. A ligand gated channel would act in milliseconds without any messenger, which describes a nicotinic synapse rather than an adrenergic one.

cards.q: Which nerve carries parasympathetic output to the heart?
cards.a: The vagus nerve.
options: The vagus nerve
The phrenic nerve
The cardiac sympathetic chain
The glossopharyngeal nerve
cards.explanation: The vagus carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to ganglia in the cardiac wall, and its postganglionic fibers reach the SA node, the AV node, and the atria. The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm and passes near the heart without innervating it. The sympathetic chain carries the opposing division. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries baroreceptor and chemoreceptor information from the carotid sinus toward the brainstem, so it is sensory input to this reflex rather than motor output to the heart.

cards.q: Which receptor does acetylcholine act on in the heart?
cards.a: The muscarinic M2 receptor.
options: The nicotinic receptor on the myocyte
The beta1 adrenergic receptor
The muscarinic M2 receptor
The muscarinic M3 receptor
cards.explanation: Vagal acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors, which couple to Gi and slow the pacemaker. Nicotinic receptors do appear in the autonomic pathway, but at the ganglionic synapse rather than on the cardiac cells themselves, which is a common mix up. Beta1 receptors respond to norepinephrine and produce the opposite effect. M3 receptors are found on glandular and smooth muscle tissue rather than on cardiac pacemaker cells.

cards.q: Besides lowering cAMP, what does M2 receptor activation do to the membrane of SA node cells?
cards.a: It opens K+ channels, so the cell hyperpolarizes.
options: It opens K+ channels, so the cell hyperpolarizes
It opens Na+ channels, so the cell depolarizes
It closes K+ channels, so the cell depolarizes
It opens Ca2+ channels, so the cell depolarizes
cards.explanation: The G protein beta gamma subunits released by M2 activation open a potassium channel directly, K+ leaves, and the cell sits further from threshold, so pacing slows on top of the slower depolarization caused by less cAMP. Opening Na+ or Ca2+ channels would depolarize the cell and speed the heart, which is the sympathetic direction. Closing K+ channels would also depolarize, so it too points the wrong way for the vagus.

cards.q: Sympathetic stimulation of the SA node increases the flow of which current during diastolic depolarization?
cards.a: The funny current, carried through HCN channels.
options: The delayed rectifier K+ current
The Na+/K+ ATPase pump current
The fast Na+ current of the ventricular action potential
The funny current, carried through HCN channels
cards.explanation: cAMP binds the HCN channel directly, increasing the inward funny current so the pacemaker potential climbs to threshold faster and the rate rises. The delayed rectifier K+ current repolarizes the cell and opposes pacing rather than driving it. The fast Na+ current is largely absent in SA node cells, which depolarize using Ca2+ instead. The Na+/K+ ATPase generates a small outward current continuously and is not the pacemaker mechanism.

cards.q: At rest, which autonomic division dominates control of heart rate?
cards.a: The parasympathetic division, through continuous vagal tone.
options: The sympathetic division, through continuous norepinephrine release
Neither, since the resting rate is purely intrinsic
The parasympathetic division, through continuous vagal tone
Both equally, so removing either has no effect
cards.explanation: The intrinsic rate of the SA node is around 100 beats per minute, yet a resting adult sits near 70, and that gap is the ongoing vagal brake. Sympathetic tone is present but modest at rest, so it is not the dominant influence. The resting rate is clearly not purely intrinsic, since it sits well below the intrinsic rate. The two divisions are not balanced equally, which is why blocking the vagus raises rate substantially.

cards.q: How does increased cAMP in SA node cells raise heart rate?
cards.a: It steepens the slope of the pacemaker potential toward threshold.
options: It lowers the threshold voltage needed for the action potential
It lengthens the plateau phase of the action potential
It makes the maximum diastolic potential more negative than usual
It steepens the slope of the pacemaker potential toward threshold
cards.explanation: More cAMP opens more HCN channels and increases Ca2+ entry during diastolic depolarization, so the membrane drifts upward faster and each interval between beats shortens. Threshold voltage itself is a property of the channels and is not the main variable moved here. A more negative maximum diastolic potential would lengthen the climb and slow the rate, which is what vagal stimulation does. The SA node action potential has no true plateau, so lengthening one is not the mechanism.

cards.q: Protein kinase A phosphorylates L type Ca2+ channels in ventricular myocytes. What is the effect on the beat?
cards.a: More Ca2+ enters and more is released, so contraction is stronger.
options: Less Ca2+ enters the cell, so the contraction is weaker
More Ca2+ enters and more is released, so contraction is stronger
More Ca2+ enters, but force is unchanged because troponin is saturated
More K+ leaves, so the cell repolarizes faster and force falls
cards.explanation: Phosphorylation increases the open probability of the L type channel, so the trigger Ca2+ entering during the plateau is larger, calcium induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is greater, and more cross bridges cycle. Less Ca2+ entry would be the effect of blocking these channels, not phosphorylating them. Troponin is not saturated at physiological calcium levels, which is exactly why extra calcium raises force. Potassium efflux is not what protein kinase A is doing here.

cards.q: Protein kinase A also phosphorylates phospholamban. What does this accomplish?
cards.a: It releases the brake on SERCA, so Ca2+ is pumped back faster.
options: It inhibits SERCA, so Ca2+ lingers and contraction is prolonged
It blocks the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, so Ca2+ accumulates in the cytosol
It opens ryanodine receptors, so Ca2+ release continues through diastole
It releases the brake on SERCA, so Ca2+ is pumped back faster
cards.explanation: Unphosphorylated phospholamban restrains SERCA, and phosphorylating it lifts that restraint so calcium is cleared from the cytosol faster, shortening relaxation and preserving filling time at high heart rates. Inhibiting SERCA would prolong contraction, the opposite of the sympathetic effect. Ryanodine receptors govern release from the store rather than reuptake into it. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes calcium from the cell and is not the target of this phosphorylation step.

cards.q: Strong vagal stimulation is applied to the SA node. Describe the change in the pacemaker potential.
cards.a: The maximum diastolic potential becomes more negative and the slope becomes shallower.
options: The maximum diastolic potential becomes more positive and the slope becomes steeper
The maximum diastolic potential becomes more negative and the slope becomes shallower
The slope steepens but the maximum diastolic potential is unchanged
The threshold voltage becomes more negative
cards.explanation: Vagal acetylcholine opens K+ channels, driving the cell further from threshold, and it lowers cAMP, which reduces the funny current so the climb toward threshold is slower, and both changes lengthen the interval between beats. A more positive starting point with a steeper slope is the sympathetic pattern. A steeper slope alone would speed the heart. Making threshold more negative would also speed the heart by shortening the distance the membrane must travel.

cards.q: A drug blocks muscarinic receptors in the heart. Predict the effect on heart rate.
cards.a: Heart rate rises, because vagal tone is removed.
options: Heart rate falls, because the sympathetic input is blocked
Heart rate rises, because contractility increases directly
Heart rate is unchanged, because the SA node sets its own rate
Heart rate rises, because vagal tone is removed
cards.explanation: The resting heart is held below its intrinsic rate by continuous vagal activity, so blocking the muscarinic receptors lifts that brake and the rate climbs toward roughly 100 beats per minute. Sympathetic transmission uses adrenergic receptors and is untouched by a muscarinic blocker. The SA node does have an intrinsic rate, but the resting rate is not that rate, which is why the drug has an effect at all. Ventricular contractility is only lightly influenced by vagal input, so it is not the route to the rate change.

cards.q: If both autonomic divisions to the heart were blocked completely, what would happen to heart rate?
cards.a: It would rise to about 100 beats per minute, the intrinsic rate of the SA node.
options: It would rise to about 100 beats per minute, the intrinsic rate of the SA node
It would fall to about 40 beats per minute
It would stop, since the heart requires neural input to beat
It would stay near 70 beats per minute, since the two divisions cancel
cards.explanation: With both influences gone, the SA node paces at its own rate of roughly 100 beats per minute, and the fact that this is faster than the resting rate reveals how much vagal restraint is normally present. About 40 beats per minute is the intrinsic rate of a ventricular escape pacemaker, which only takes over if the SA node fails. The heart beats without any innervation at all, as a transplanted heart demonstrates. The two divisions are not balanced, so removing both does not leave the rate where it was.

cards.q: A beta1 blocker is given to a patient at rest. Predict the effects on heart rate and on contractility.
cards.a: Both fall, since beta1 receptors mediate each effect.
options: Heart rate falls but contractility rises instead
Both rise, since blocking a receptor removes inhibition
Heart rate rises but contractility falls instead
Both fall, since beta1 receptors mediate each effect
cards.explanation: Beta1 receptors carry sympathetic drive to both the SA node, where they speed pacing, and the ventricular myocytes, where they raise force, so blocking them slows the rate and weakens the beat together. Contractility cannot rise when the receptor that raises it is blocked. Heart rate cannot rise from removing a stimulatory input. Beta1 receptors are excitatory rather than inhibitory, so blocking them removes stimulation rather than releasing a brake.

cards.q: Trace the sequence from norepinephrine binding a ventricular beta1 receptor to a change in end systolic volume.
cards.a: Gs raises cAMP, Ca2+ entry and release increase, and end systolic volume falls.
options: Gi lowers cAMP, less Ca2+ enters, force falls, and end systolic volume rises
Gs raises cAMP, venous return increases, preload rises, and end systolic volume falls
Gq raises IP3, Ca2+ leaves the cell, force rises, and end systolic volume rises
Gs raises cAMP, Ca2+ entry and release increase, and end systolic volume falls
cards.explanation: The beta1 receptor couples to Gs, and the resulting cAMP and protein kinase A activity increases calcium entry and release so the ventricle contracts more forcefully, empties further, and leaves a smaller residual volume. The Gi pathway with falling cAMP belongs to muscarinic receptors and produces the opposite result. The Gq pathway belongs to alpha1 receptors on vessels, and calcium leaving the cell would weaken rather than strengthen contraction. An answer that smuggles in a venous return change misses the point, since beta1 receptors on the ventricle act on contractility, not on filling.

cards.q: At the start of exercise, heart rate climbs from 70 to about 100 beats per minute within a few seconds, faster than circulating catecholamines could act. What explains this initial rise, and what carries the rise beyond 100?
cards.a: Withdrawal of vagal tone produces the first rise, and increasing sympathetic activity carries the rate higher.
options: Withdrawal of vagal tone produces the first rise, and increasing sympathetic activity carries the rate higher
Increased sympathetic activity produces the first rise, and vagal withdrawal carries the rate higher
Rising body temperature produces both parts of the rise
Increased venous return raises the rate directly through stretch of the SA node
cards.explanation: Because vagal tone holds the resting rate below the intrinsic rate of about 100, simply releasing that brake gets the heart to 100 quickly, and neural withdrawal acts within a beat or two. Anything faster than that must be sympathetic activation, which then drives the rate well above the intrinsic value. Reversing the order cannot explain a rise that stops near the intrinsic rate, and temperature rises far too slowly to account for a change within seconds. Atrial stretch does nudge the rate, but it is a small contributor compared with the autonomic shift.

cards.q: A compound inhibits the phosphodiesterase that breaks down cAMP in cardiac cells. Predict the effects on heart rate and contractility, and explain why.
cards.a: Both rise, because cAMP accumulates and acts as beta1 stimulation would.
options: Both fall, because cAMP is an inhibitory messenger in the heart
Heart rate rises but contractility falls, since cAMP acts only on the SA node
Both rise, because cAMP accumulates and acts as beta1 stimulation would
Neither changes, because the beta1 receptor itself was not activated
cards.explanation: Blocking the enzyme that destroys cAMP lets the messenger build up, and the downstream consequences are the same whether the cAMP came from a stimulated receptor or from reduced breakdown, so the funny current increases at the SA node and calcium handling improves in the ventricle. cAMP is stimulatory in the heart, not inhibitory. It acts in both pacemaker and contractile cells, so restricting its effect to rate alone is incorrect. Bypassing the receptor is exactly the point of acting on the messenger instead.

cards.q: A compound selectively blocks HCN channels in the SA node without affecting ventricular calcium handling. Predict the effect on heart rate, contractility, stroke volume, and cardiac output.
cards.a: Heart rate falls, contractility is unchanged, stroke volume rises, and output falls slightly.
options: Heart rate falls, contractility falls, stroke volume falls, and cardiac output falls sharply
Heart rate falls, contractility is unchanged, stroke volume rises, and output falls slightly
Heart rate rises, contractility is unchanged, and cardiac output rises
Heart rate falls, contractility rises to compensate, and cardiac output is unchanged
cards.explanation: Blocking the funny current flattens the pacemaker potential so the SA node fires less often, but the ventricular myocyte is untouched, so force at any given length is the same. The slower rate lengthens diastole, filling increases, and Frank Starling raises stroke volume, which partly offsets the rate reduction, so output drops less than the rate does. Contractility cannot fall when ventricular calcium handling is spared, and it does not rise on its own without sympathetic drive. Blocking an inward pacemaker current cannot raise the rate.

cards.q: Where is the aortic auscultation area located?
cards.a: The second intercostal space at the right sternal border.
options: The fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
The second intercostal space at the left sternal border
The second intercostal space at the right sternal border
The fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
cards.explanation: Sound from the aortic valve carries along the direction of blood flow into the ascending aorta, which travels up and to the right, so it is heard best at the right second intercostal space. The left second intercostal space is the pulmonic area. The fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line is the mitral area at the apex. The left lower sternal border is the tricuspid area.

cards.q: Where is the pulmonic auscultation area located?
cards.a: The second intercostal space at the left sternal border.
options: The second intercostal space at the right sternal border
The second intercostal space at the left sternal border
The fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
The xiphoid process
cards.explanation: The pulmonary trunk runs up and slightly to the left, so pulmonic valve sounds project to the left second intercostal space. The right second intercostal space belongs to the aortic valve, and confusing the two sides is the most common error in this exercise. The apex at the fifth intercostal space midclavicular line is where mitral sounds are loudest. The xiphoid process is not one of the four standard listening areas.

cards.q: Where is the tricuspid auscultation area located?
cards.a: The fourth or fifth intercostal space at the lower left sternal border.
options: The second intercostal space at the left sternal border
The second intercostal space at the right sternal border
The fifth intercostal space at the left anterior axillary line
The fourth or fifth intercostal space at the lower left sternal border
cards.explanation: The tricuspid valve sits behind the lower sternum, so its sounds are heard best just beside the sternum at the fourth or fifth interspace. The left second interspace is the pulmonic area, higher on the chest. The anterior axillary line is lateral to the apex and is not a standard area, although mitral murmurs may radiate that way. The right second interspace is the aortic area.

cards.q: Where is the mitral auscultation area located?
cards.a: The fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line.
options: The fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
The third intercostal space at the left sternal border
The fifth intercostal space at the right sternal border
The second intercostal space at the left sternal border
cards.explanation: The apex of the heart points down and to the left and sits at the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, which is where mitral sounds are loudest and where the apical impulse is felt. The third left interspace is above the apex and is sometimes used as a secondary listening point but is not the mitral area. The right side of the chest at that level is far from the apex. The left second interspace is the pulmonic area.

cards.q: Which part of the stethoscope is used for low pitched sounds such as a third heart sound?
cards.a: The bell, applied lightly.
options: The diaphragm, pressed firmly
The bell, applied lightly
The diaphragm, applied lightly
Either one, since the pieces perform identically
cards.explanation: The bell transmits low frequencies when it rests lightly on the skin, because firm pressure stretches the skin into a diaphragm and filters those frequencies out. The diaphragm is built to favor higher pitched sounds such as the first and second sounds and most murmurs. Applying the diaphragm lightly does not turn it into a bell. The two pieces have genuinely different frequency responses, which is why both exist.

cards.q: Which part of the stethoscope is best for hearing the first and second heart sounds?
cards.a: The diaphragm.
options: The bell
The tubing pressed against the chest
The diaphragm
The earpieces reversed to face backward
cards.explanation: The first and second sounds are relatively high pitched snapping sounds, and the diaphragm favors exactly that frequency range. The bell is reserved for low pitched findings such as third and fourth heart sounds and the murmur of mitral stenosis. Tubing pressed against the chest picks up no useful signal and adds noise. Earpieces should point forward along the ear canals, and reversing them blocks the sound rather than improving it.

cards.q: Where is the point of maximal impulse normally palpated?
cards.a: The fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line.
options: The fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
Directly over the sternum
The second intercostal space at the left sternal border
The fifth intercostal space at the right midclavicular line
cards.explanation: The apex strikes the chest wall during contraction at the fifth interspace in the midclavicular line, the same place the mitral area is auscultated. The left second interspace overlies the great vessels rather than the apex. The sternum covers the right ventricle and the septum, and the impulse there is not the apical beat. The apex points to the left, so the right midclavicular line is on the wrong side of the chest.

cards.q: Which pulse is used to time heart sounds during auscultation?
cards.a: The carotid pulse.
options: The radial pulse
The dorsalis pedis pulse
The carotid pulse
The popliteal pulse
cards.explanation: The carotid artery is close to the heart, so its upstroke arrives almost immediately after ejection begins and lines up usefully with the first heart sound. The radial pulse is measurably delayed by the travel time out the arm, so it can mislead timing at fast rates. The dorsalis pedis and popliteal pulses are even further away and arrive later still. Distance from the aortic valve is the whole basis for the choice.

cards.q: During auscultation, a sound is heard at the same moment the carotid pulse is felt. Which sound is it?
cards.a: The first heart sound.
options: The second heart sound
The first heart sound
A third heart sound
A fourth heart sound
cards.explanation: The carotid upstroke is produced by ejection, which begins a fraction of a second after the AV valves close, so the sound that coincides with the pulse is the first sound. The second sound ends ejection and arrives after the carotid upstroke has already passed. A third sound falls in early diastole, well after the pulse. A fourth sound falls just before the first sound and therefore just before the pulse.

cards.q: A student feels the carotid pulse while listening and hears a murmur that occupies the interval containing that pulse. How should the murmur be classified?
cards.a: Systolic.
options: Diastolic
Systolic
Presystolic
Continuous
cards.explanation: The carotid upstroke happens during ejection, which is part of ventricular systole, so a murmur filling that same interval is systolic. A diastolic murmur would fall in the interval after the pulse has subsided and before the next upstroke. Presystolic refers to the moment just before the first sound, during atrial contraction. A continuous murmur would not stop at the second sound and would span both intervals.

cards.q: Why is each valve area located downstream of the valve rather than directly over it?
cards.a: Sound travels in the direction that blood is flowing.
options: The stethoscope only detects sound at the skin surface over bone
The ribs block sound directly over each valve
The valves are too deep to hear at all
Sound travels in the direction that blood is flowing
cards.explanation: Vibrations generated at a valve are carried along the moving column of blood, so the loudest point on the chest wall lies in the path of that flow, which is why aortic sounds project up and right and mitral sounds project down and left. The ribs do transmit sound imperfectly, but the listening areas were chosen by flow direction rather than by rib position. The valves are certainly audible, which is the premise of the exercise. Sound is transmitted through soft tissue as well as bone.

cards.q: Why is the radial pulse a poor choice for timing heart sounds at a high heart rate?
cards.a: The pressure wave takes time to reach the wrist, so it lags.
options: The radial artery does not pulsate strongly during systole
The radial artery is compressed by the stethoscope tubing
The radial pulse reflects diastolic pressure rather than systolic
The pressure wave takes time to reach the wrist, so it lags
cards.explanation: The pulse wave has to travel from the aortic root all the way down the arm, and by the time it arrives the heart may already be well into the next part of the cycle, so at fast rates the lag can point you at the wrong sound. The radial artery does pulsate with each ejection, so a claim that it does not is simply incorrect. The pulse reflects the systolic upstroke, not diastolic pressure. The stethoscope is on the chest and does not compress the wrist.

cards.q: A pulse deficit is found when the apical rate exceeds the radial rate. What does this indicate?
cards.a: Some contractions are too weak to produce a palpable pulse.
options: Some contractions are too weak to produce a palpable pulse
The radial artery is partly occluded by atherosclerosis
The examiner is counting the second heart sound as a separate beat
The heart is beating faster on the left than on the right
cards.explanation: Every audible beat at the apex represents a ventricular contraction, but a contraction that follows too soon after the previous one has had little filling time and may eject too little blood to raise a palpable wave at the wrist, so the counts diverge. A localized arterial blockage is possible but would be an unusual cause and would not fluctuate beat to beat. Miscounting sounds is an error to rule out but is not what the term describes. The two ventricles necessarily beat at the same rate.

cards.q: A student counts an apical rate of 96 beats per minute and a radial rate of 78 beats per minute over the same minute. What is the pulse deficit?
cards.a: 18 beats per minute.
options: 78 beats per minute
174 beats per minute
18 beats per minute
8 beats per minute
cards.explanation: The deficit is the apical rate minus the radial rate, so 96 minus 78 is 18 beats per minute that did not produce a palpable wrist pulse. The value 174 comes from adding the two counts, which double counts every beat. The value 78 is the radial rate itself. The value 8 does not follow from either operation and would come from a subtraction error.

cards.q: In a resting subject, a student notices two unequal pauses between sounds. Which interval is diastole?
cards.a: The longer pause, running from the second sound to the next first sound.
options: The shorter pause, running from the first sound to the second sound
The two pauses are equal at rest, so neither can be identified
The longer pause, running from the second sound to the next first sound
The longer pause, running from the first sound to the second sound
cards.explanation: Systole runs from AV valve closure at the first sound to semilunar closure at the second sound, and at rest it fills only about a third of the cycle, so the gap back to the next first sound is longer and is diastole. The shorter interval bounded by the two sounds is systole. The pauses are clearly unequal at a resting rate, which is what makes this cue usable. The interval from the first to the second sound is by definition the shorter one at rest.

cards.q: At the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line, a student hears a blowing sound that begins with the first sound and continues to the second sound, and the carotid pulse coincides with it. Which valve is involved and what is the lesion?
cards.a: The mitral valve, with regurgitation, since it leaks while it should be sealed.
options: The aortic valve, with stenosis, since the sound is loudest over the apex
The mitral valve, with regurgitation, since it leaks while it should be sealed
The mitral valve, with stenosis, since it is obstructing flow during systole
The tricuspid valve, with regurgitation, since the apex overlies the right ventricle
cards.explanation: The location identifies the mitral valve, and the timing with the carotid pulse places the sound in systole, when the mitral valve should be closed, so blood is escaping backward through a valve that fails to seal. Aortic stenosis is also systolic but is loudest at the right second interspace and radiates to the neck rather than centering at the apex. Mitral stenosis obstructs filling, which occurs in diastole, so its murmur would fall in the other interval. The apex overlies the left ventricle, not the right.

cards.q: At the right second intercostal space, a harsh sound fills the interval between the first and second sounds and radiates toward the neck. Which valve is involved, and during which cardiac cycle phase is the sound produced?
cards.a: The aortic valve, with the sound produced during ventricular ejection.
options: The pulmonic valve, with the sound produced during ventricular ejection
The aortic valve, with the sound produced during isovolumetric contraction
The mitral valve, with the sound produced during ventricular filling
The aortic valve, with the sound produced during ventricular ejection
cards.explanation: The right second interspace with radiation toward the carotids is the aortic area, and a sound between the first and second sounds occupies systole, but within systole the only phase carrying flow through the aortic valve is ejection, since no blood moves during isovolumetric contraction. The pulmonic valve projects to the left second interspace instead. A mitral filling sound would fall in diastole, after the second sound. Naming isovolumetric contraction is a useful trap, because it is systolic but has no flow to make turbulence.

cards.q: A student auscultating a subject at 180 beats per minute cannot tell the first sound from the second by rhythm. What should the student do, and why does the problem arise?
cards.a: Palpate the carotid pulse while listening, because diastole shortens at high rates.
options: Palpate the radial pulse while listening, because it arrives at the same instant as the first sound
Count only the louder sound, because the first sound is always louder at high rates
Switch to the bell, because high rates raise the pitch of both sounds
Palpate the carotid pulse while listening, because diastole shortens at high rates
cards.explanation: The rhythmic cue depends on diastole being clearly longer than systole, and speeding the heart takes its time mainly out of diastole, so the two intervals converge and the cue fails. The carotid upstroke still marks ejection, so feeling it identifies the first sound directly. The radial pulse lags by the travel time down the arm, which is precisely the error to avoid at fast rates. Switching to the bell changes which frequencies you hear rather than which sound is which, and loudness varies too much with the subject and the site to be reliable.

cards.q: A student hears the first sound at the apex, feels the carotid upstroke an instant later, and then hears the second sound. Put these three events in order against the cardiac cycle.
cards.a: AV valves close, then ejection produces the carotid upstroke, then the aortic valve closes.
options: The aortic valve opens, then the AV valves close, then ejection produces the carotid upstroke
AV valves close, then the aortic valve closes, then ejection produces the carotid upstroke
The carotid upstroke occurs first, then the AV valves close, then ejection begins
AV valves close, then ejection produces the carotid upstroke, then the aortic valve closes
cards.explanation: The first sound is AV valve closure, and the short delay before the pulse arrives is isovolumetric contraction, the time the ventricle spends building pressure before the aortic valve can open. Ejection then sends the pressure wave to the carotid, and the second sound marks aortic closure ending ejection. The aortic valve cannot open before the AV valves close, since that would let blood move in both directions at once, and the carotid upstroke requires ejection so it cannot precede the first sound. Ejection must precede aortic valve closure rather than follow it.
